historicalNotes.title: The Popular Electronics Cover
historicalNotes.text: The January 1975 issue of Popular Electronics featuring the Altair 8800 is considered one of the most consequential magazine covers in technology history. MITS was flooded with thousands of orders, saving Ed Roberts' struggling calculator company from bankruptcy.

historicalNotes.title: Birth of Microsoft
historicalNotes.text: Paul Allen spotted the Popular Electronics cover at a newsstand in Harvard Square and showed it to Bill Gates. Within weeks, they had written a BASIC interpreter for the Altair - despite not having access to the actual hardware. They demonstrated it to Ed Roberts in Albuquerque, and Microsoft was born.

overview: The MITS Altair 8800, featured on the cover of Popular Electronics in January 1975, is widely regarded as the spark that ignited the personal computer revolution. Designed by Ed Roberts in Albuquerque, New Mexico, this kit computer used the Intel 8080 processor and featured a front panel of toggle switches and LEDs - there was no keyboard, no screen, and no storage in the base configuration. Despite its primitive interface, the Altair generated enormous excitement among hobbyists. It also inspired a young Bill Gates and Paul Allen to write Altair BASIC, the first product of their new company, Micro-Soft. The Altair's S-100 bus became an industry standard that shaped the early microcomputer industry.

overview: The IMSAI 8080 was the first clone of the MITS Altair 8800 and became one of the most successful S-100 bus computers of the late 1970s. Founded by Bill Millard's IMS Associates in San Leandro, California, the IMSAI improved on the Altair with a more robust power supply, better build quality, and a distinctive blue and red front panel that became iconic. The IMSAI 8080 gained lasting pop culture fame through its appearance in the 1983 film WarGames, where Matthew Broderick's character used one to accidentally hack into a military supercomputer. With CP/M and floppy drives, the IMSAI became a capable business machine and helped establish the S-100 ecosystem.

historicalNotes.title: The Byte Shop Deal
historicalNotes.text: Paul Terrell, owner of the Byte Shop in Mountain View, ordered 50 Apple I boards at $500 each - but he wanted them fully assembled, not as kits. Steve Jobs scrambled to fulfill the order, buying parts on 30-day credit. This single order transformed Apple from a garage hobby into a real business.

historicalNotes.title: Million-Dollar Collectible
historicalNotes.text: With only about 60-70 Apple I units believed to survive, they have become the most valuable collectible computers in history. A working unit sold at auction in 2014 for $905,000. The original price of $666.66 was chosen by Wozniak simply because he liked repeating digits.

overview: The Apple I, designed and hand-built by Steve Wozniak in 1976, was the founding product of Apple Computer. Unlike other hobbyist kits of the era, it came as a fully assembled circuit board - though buyers still needed to supply their own case, keyboard, and display. Just 200 units were built, most sold through Paul Terrell's Byte Shop in Mountain View, California. The Apple I featured a MOS 6502 processor and included a built-in video terminal interface, a significant advance over the front-panel switches of the Altair. Today, surviving units are among the most valuable collectible computers in the world, with auction prices exceeding $900,000.

historicalNotes.title: The 6502 Demo Board
historicalNotes.text: The KIM-1 was originally designed by Chuck Peddle and his team at MOS Technology as a development board to demonstrate the capabilities of their new 6502 processor. It was never intended to be a consumer product, but demand from hobbyists was so strong that MOS Technology began selling it directly. At $245, it was far cheaper than the Altair 8800 and offered a more user-friendly experience with its built-in keypad and LED display.

historicalNotes.title: Commodore Acquisition
historicalNotes.text: When Commodore Business Machines acquired MOS Technology in 1976, the KIM-1 became a Commodore product. The technology and engineering team that created the KIM-1 would go on to design the Commodore PET, VIC-20, and Commodore 64 - a direct lineage from this humble single-board computer to some of the best-selling home computers of all time.

historicalNotes.title: Modern Recreations
historicalNotes.text: The KIM-1's elegant simplicity has inspired numerous modern recreations. Boards like the PAL-1, KIM Uno, and others allow enthusiasts to experience 6502 programming on authentic-feeling hardware. The VirtualKim app provides a faithful software emulation of the KIM-1, letting users program in machine code on their iPhone or iPad.

overview: The KIM-1 (Keyboard Input Monitor), released in 1976 by MOS Technology, was one of the most important early microcomputers. Originally designed as a demonstration board for the MOS 6502 processor, it quickly became a popular computer in its own right. For just $245, users got a single-board computer with a 6502 running at 1 MHz, 1 KB of RAM, 2 KB of ROM containing a monitor program, a 23-key hexadecimal keypad, and a 6-digit LED display. It also included a cassette interface and 15 I/O pins via two 6530 RRIOT (ROM-RAM-I/O-Timer) chips. After Commodore acquired MOS Technology in 1976, the KIM-1 continued in production and inspired a wave of single-board computers. Its simplicity and low cost made it ideal for learning machine language programming, and many hobbyists and engineers cut their teeth on the KIM-1. It remains popular today with recreations and emulators keeping the platform alive. The user's own app, VirtualKim, provides a faithful emulation of the KIM-1.

historicalNotes.text: Steve Wozniak designed virtually every component of the Apple II single-handedly, including the ingenious floppy disk controller that used just 8 chips where competitors needed 50+. His elegant engineering made the Apple II both affordable and reliable.
historicalNotes.title: The Wozniak Genius

historicalNotes.text: Dan Bricklin and Bob Frankston's VisiCalc spreadsheet, released in 1979 exclusively for the Apple II, transformed the computer from a hobbyist toy into an essential business tool. It's often called the first 'killer app' - businesses bought Apple IIs specifically to run VisiCalc.
historicalNotes.title: VisiCalc Changes Everything

historicalNotes.text: The Apple II spawned six major models over 11 years. The II Plus (1979) added Applesoft BASIC. The IIe (1983) became the education standard with its 11-year production run. The portable IIc (1984) and its faster IIc Plus (1988) brought the platform to desktops and (large) briefcases alike. The IIgs (1986) was the pinnacle - a 16-bit machine with Ensoniq wavetable sound that could have competed with the Amiga and Atari ST, but Apple deliberately (allegedly) limited its clock speed to avoid cannibalizing Macintosh sales.
historicalNotes.title: The Apple II Family Tree

historicalNotes.text: The Apple II enjoys one of the most active modern hardware scenes of any vintage computer. The A2Pico, based on the Raspberry Pi Pico, is a multi-function peripheral card that can be reprogrammed to serve as SD card storage, a Z80 CP/M coprocessor, or a mouse interface. A2Heaven produces the MockingBoard-T, a faithful recreation of the beloved Mockingboard sound card that adds AY-3-8913 synthesiser audio, plus SD-based floppy emulators and VGA output cards. The A2FPGA from ReActiveMicro combines HDMI video output and full Mockingboard sound emulation in a single slot. Joe's Computer Museum (jcm-1.com) offers the MiniPerformer+, an accelerator board for the Mac Plus, plus replacement chips and repair parts. Even the SPIISD provides simple SD card storage with an OLED display for selecting disk images. These projects keep the Apple II not just alive but actively evolving.
historicalNotes.title: A Renaissance in Modern Hardware

overview:
The Apple II, designed primarily by Steve Wozniak and introduced in 1977, was one of the first highly successful mass-produced microcomputers. It featured color graphics, a built-in BASIC interpreter, and eight expansion slots that made it enormously versatile. The Apple II became the standard computer in American schools and, with the addition of VisiCalc - the first spreadsheet program - it became a serious business tool. Its open architecture and extensive expansion options fostered a thriving ecosystem of hardware and software that sustained the platform for over 15 years.

The Apple II family grew through a remarkable series of models. The Apple II Plus (1979) added Applesoft BASIC in ROM, replacing the original Integer BASIC and making floating-point math accessible out of the box. The Apple IIe (1983) became the workhorse of the line, adding uppercase and lowercase text, a full 64 KB of RAM, and the auxiliary slot for 80-column display and double hi-res graphics - it remained in production until November 1993, an extraordinary 11-year run. The Apple IIc (1984) repackaged the IIe into a compact, portable form factor with built-in floppy drive, 128 KB RAM, and serial ports, aiming for the portable market. The Apple IIgs (1986) was the most powerful of the family, featuring a 16-bit 65C816 processor, the Ensoniq 5503 wavetable synthesizer for stunning audio, a super hi-res 4096-color graphics mode, and a Mac-like graphical desktop. Finally, the Apple IIc Plus (1988) updated the compact IIc with a faster 4 MHz 65C02 processor and a built-in 3.5-inch floppy drive, making it the last Apple II model introduced before Apple shifted focus entirely to the Macintosh line.

historicalNotes.text: The PET 2001 debuted alongside the Apple II and TRS-80 as one of the three machines later dubbed the '1977 Trinity.' Much of its DNA came from Chuck Peddle and the MOS Technology team behind the KIM-1, who turned a 6502-based engineering culture into one of the first mass-market personal computers.
historicalNotes.title: One of the 1977 Trinity

historicalNotes.text: Early PET models shipped with a tiny 'chiclet' keyboard that looked futuristic but frustrated serious typists almost immediately. Commodore had to respond with full-travel business keyboards, and the original PET keyboard became one of the classic cautionary tales in computer industrial design.
historicalNotes.title: The Chiclet Keyboard Backlash

historicalNotes.text: The PET became especially strong in education, with heavy adoption in schools across Canada and parts of Europe thanks to its all-in-one metal case and reliable disk-drive ecosystem. Commodore's use of the IEEE-488 bus also gave PET systems unusually robust, fast peripheral connections compared with the cassette- and serial-centric setups common on home computers.
historicalNotes.title: Schools and the IEEE-488 Edge

overview: The Commodore PET (Personal Electronic Transactor) was one of the "1977 Trinity" of personal computers alongside the Apple II and TRS-80. Designed by Chuck Peddle - the same engineer who created the 6502 CPU - the PET featured an all-in-one design with built-in monitor, cassette drive, and a distinctive calculator-style keyboard (later replaced with a full keyboard). It became hugely popular in Canadian and European schools and established Commodore as a major force in personal computing.

historicalNotes.text: The Nascom 1 represented the peak of the British kit computer era. Buyers received a bag of components and a PCB, and had to solder hundreds of connections. The build process could take an experienced hobbyist an entire weekend, and a single cold solder joint could mean hours of debugging.
historicalNotes.title: The Kit Computer Era

historicalNotes.text: The International Nascom Micro Computer club (INMC) was one of the most active early computer user groups in the UK. They published a regular newsletter, organized meetings, and maintained a library of software on cassette tape. The community spirit of the INMC helped many first-time computer owners get started.

overview: The Nascom 1, released in 1977, was one of the earliest British single-board computers available in kit form. Designed by the team at Nasco Trading, it was based on the Zilog Z80 processor and came as a bag of components with a professionally manufactured PCB. Builders needed to solder every component themselves, making it a true hobbyist machine. Despite its spartan design - just a bare circuit board with a keyboard - the Nascom developed a passionate following and an active user group that produced software and hardware expansions. It was an important stepping stone in British home computing, predating the ZX80 by three years.

historicalNotes.title: Radio Shack's Surprise Bestseller
historicalNotes.text: The TRS-80 was sold through thousands of Radio Shack stores, putting a real computer in malls and shopping centers where most Americans had never seen one for sale. Tandy expected modest demand, but the machine became an immediate hit and helped define the mass-market personal computer business.

historicalNotes.title: From 'Trash-80' to BASIC Workhorse
historicalNotes.text: Critics and fans alike nicknamed it the 'Trash-80,' a jab at both 'TRS' and Radio Shack's mass-market image. Early units shipped with Level I BASIC, derived from Tiny BASIC, but many users quickly upgraded to the far more capable Level II BASIC from Microsoft, which made the machine much more practical for serious programming.

historicalNotes.title: A Platform That Grew Up
historicalNotes.text: What began as a simple Z80 home computer evolved into an entire family: the original Model I, the better-shielded all-in-one Model III, and the more capable Model 4 with stronger business and CP/M support. Along the way, the TRS-80 built a substantial software ecosystem of word processors, accounting packages, and other small-business tools.

photos.caption: A TRS-80 Model I in a museum collection - preserved for future generations
The TRS-80 keyboard - Radio Shack's entry into personal computing

overview: The TRS-80 Model I, manufactured by Tandy Corporation and sold through their Radio Shack stores, was one of the best-selling computers of 1977-78. At $599 it undercut the Apple II significantly. It used a Z80 processor with 4 KB of RAM (expandable to 48 KB) and Level I BASIC in ROM. Despite its monochrome display and limited graphics, it built a substantial software library. Its ready availability through Radio Shack's nationwide chain of stores was a key advantage - at a time when buying a computer usually meant ordering by mail.

historicalNotes.title: The Signetics 2650
historicalNotes.text: The 2650 processor at the heart of the Instructor 50 had a fascinating history. Designed in 1972 by John Kessler, formerly of IBM, it was modeled on the IBM 1130 minicomputer and was one of the most sophisticated microprocessor designs of its time. However, Signetics delayed its release until 1975 due to their work with Dolby Laboratories on noise-reduction ICs. By then, the Intel 8080 and Motorola 6800 had established themselves, and the 2650 - despite its elegant architecture with bank-switched registers and vectored interrupts - never achieved widespread adoption. Philips acquired Signetics in 1975, and versions of the 2650 can be found with both Signetics and Philips branding.

historicalNotes.title: Educational Excellence
historicalNotes.text: The Instructor 50's greatest legacy may be its remarkable course materials. The five-volume set of ring-bound course books formed a complete self-study course on microprocessor programming, taking students from basic concepts through to advanced topics like DMA and interrupt priority systems. All figures were printed on fold-out pages so students could reference diagrams while reading. These books are widely considered among the finest educational materials ever produced for learning assembly language programming, and remain sought-after by collectors.

photos.caption: The original magazine advert for the Signetics Instructor 50

overview: The Signetics Instructor 50 (1978) was a single-board training computer designed to teach the architecture and programming of the Signetics 2650 microprocessor. Built by Signetics - a Sunnyvale, California chip company that became a subsidiary of Philips in 1975 - it was aimed squarely at the educational market. For around $200, students received a complete self-contained system with a 2650A processor running at 895 kHz, 640 bytes of RAM (512 available to the user), a 2 KB ROM containing the USE (User System Executive) monitor, an 8-digit LED display that greeted users with "HELLO" on power-up, a hexadecimal keypad for entering machine code, and 8 toggle switches with corresponding LEDs for I/O experimentation. Unlike many trainer boards of the era, the Instructor 50 included a cassette interface for program storage and an S-100 compatible expansion bus, making it a surprisingly capable little system. Signetics accompanied it with an exceptional set of five course books that formed a complete self-study course on microprocessor programming - widely regarded as some of the best educational material produced for any 8-bit processor. The 2650 itself was an interesting CPU designed by John Kessler, modeled on the IBM 1130 minicomputer, featuring 7 general-purpose registers with bank switching, vectored interrupts, and BCD arithmetic - minicomputer features rarely seen on 1970s microprocessors.

keyFeatures: Widely adopted in British schools before BBC Micro

historicalNotes.title: Before the BBC Micro
historicalNotes.text: Before the BBC Micro arrived in 1981, Research Machines was the dominant supplier of computers to British schools. The 380Z and its successors gave many British students their first experience of computing. RM continued as a major educational technology supplier well into the 21st century.

historicalNotes.title: A 1977 Education Workhorse
historicalNotes.text: Introduced in 1977, the 380Z belongs to the era before the great British home-computer boom. It was aimed at schools, laboratories, and business users rather than at the living-room gaming market that defined the 1980s.

historicalNotes.title: More Professional Than Hobbyist
historicalNotes.text: With its proper keyboard, monitor options, and disk-oriented software, the 380Z felt closer to a small business system than to the build-it-yourself micros many hobbyists knew. That seriousness was a big part of its appeal to teachers and administrators.

photos.caption: The Research Machines 380Z - a tank and UK classroom staple of the early 1980s
Research Machines 380Z front view. Photo: Paul Flo Williams, CC BY 3.0
Research Machines 380Z rear panel and connectors. Photo: Paul Flo Williams, CC BY 3.0
Inside the Research Machines 380Z. Photo: Paul Flo Williams, CC BY 3.0

overview: The Research Machines 380Z, introduced in 1978, was one of the most important educational computers in British history, predating the BBC Micro's dominance in UK schools. Manufactured by Research Machines Limited (RM) in Oxford, it used a Z80A processor running at 4 MHz with up to 56 KB of RAM. The 380Z was built to rugged standards suitable for classroom use, with a metal case and reliable construction that justified its relatively high price of around £3,000. It ran CP/M and had its own BASIC interpreter, and was widely adopted by British schools, polytechnics, and universities throughout the late 1970s and early 1980s. RM went on to become one of the UK's most important educational technology companies, a position they maintained for decades.

historicalNotes.title: Sharp's Clean Computer
historicalNotes.text: The MZ-80K embodied Sharp's 'clean computer' philosophy: instead of booting straight into ROM BASIC, it started with only a monitor program and loaded languages from cassette. That made it feel more like a flexible computing platform than a fixed appliance.

historicalNotes.title: An All-in-One Pioneer
historicalNotes.text: With its built-in monitor, keyboard, and cassette deck, the MZ-80K was unusually self-contained for 1978. The design made early personal computing look less like a bag of parts and more like a complete product for homes, schools, and small offices.

photos.caption: The Sharp MZ-2000, an evolution of the MZ-80 range intended for business users

overview: The Sharp MZ-80K, released in 1978, was one of Japan's earliest personal computers. It took a "clean computer" approach - the machine contained only a monitor ROM and loaded its operating system and BASIC interpreter from cassette tape. This meant different languages and operating systems could be loaded, making it unusually flexible. The built-in cassette deck and green monochrome monitor made it a self-contained unit. The MZ-80K established Sharp as a major player in the Japanese personal computer market.

historicalNotes.title: The Practical Electronics Phenomenon
historicalNotes.text: The MK14 reached thousands of British hobbyists through magazine coverage and mail-order kit sales, presenting a real microcomputer as something an ordinary enthusiast could actually build. For many owners it was the first processor-based machine they had ever touched.

historicalNotes.title: Machine Code Before BASIC
historicalNotes.text: With its hex keypad and seven-segment LED display, the MK14 was really a microprocessor trainer rather than a friendly home computer. Owners learned to think in opcodes, memory addresses, and interface circuits - an education that shaped a generation of British hardware hackers.

historicalNotes.title: Science of Cambridge's Debut
historicalNotes.text: Released in 1978 by Science of Cambridge, the MK14 came before the ZX80 and established the low-cost mail-order formula Clive Sinclair would use again with later machines. It was Sinclair's first step into personal computing.

photos.caption: Annotated view of the Science of Cambridge MK14 circuit board

overview: The Science of Cambridge MK14 (1978) was Clive Sinclair's first computer product, designed by Ian Williamson. Based on the National Semiconductor INS8060 (SC/MP) processor with just 256 bytes of RAM and a hex keypad with LED display. Sold as a kit for £39.95, it introduced many enthusiasts to microprocessors. Despite its minimal capabilities, around 50,000 were sold, proving there was a market for affordable home computing kits in the UK.

historicalNotes.title: A Lower-Cost Atari
historicalNotes.text: The 400 and 800 shared Atari's custom-chip architecture, but the 400 cut costs with a membrane keyboard, one cartridge slot, and less accessible internal expansion. It was a home computer with an operating system and programming cartridges, not an Atari 2600 console.

historicalNotes.title: From 8 KB to More Useful Memory
historicalNotes.text: Atari's 1980 brochure lists 8 KB of RAM for both the 400 and 800. It offers a service-center upgrade to 16 KB for the 400 and specifies at least 16 KB for disk-drive use. Later 400s shipped with 16 KB, and service-center or third-party upgrades could take the machine to 48 KB.

historicalNotes.title: CTIA and GTIA Revisions
historicalNotes.text: The original CTIA hardware used a 128-color palette, not 128 simultaneous playfield colors. GTIA appeared in new 400 and 800 computers in early 1982. Its additional 80×192 modes include 16 shades of one hue; the catalog's 16-color game statistic represents these later factory-equipped machines, not every 1979 example.

overview:
The Atari 400 reached the market in late 1979 as the lower-cost member of Atari's first home-computer range, initially priced at $549.95 in the United States. Its flat membrane keyboard and single cartridge slot distinguished it from the larger Atari 800. The wipe-clean keyboard suited family use and games, but was less comfortable for sustained typing than the 800's full-travel keys.

Early machines shipped with 8 KB of RAM, despite the model name's reference to an earlier 4 KB design target. Later units had 16 KB; expansion required service work rather than the 800's user-accessible memory modules. The 10 KB operating-system ROM was separate from the Atari BASIC cartridge. A television connected through RF, with no dedicated composite monitor socket on the standard 400.

The 400 shared the 800's 6502-family processor, ANTIC display processor, POKEY sound, four controller ports, and SIO peripheral bus. Early examples used CTIA video; later production gained GTIA and its extra graphics modes, including 16 shades at 80×192. Software compatibility depends on RAM, operating-system revision, and video hardware, not just the shared Atari name.

historicalNotes.title: The Expandable Model
historicalNotes.text: The 800's full-travel keyboard and accessible memory modules made it more convenient for programming and writing than the 400. Atari's 1980 brochure specifies 8 KB of base RAM and user-installed expansion to 48 KB, so the later common 48 KB configuration should not be mistaken for the original base specification.

historicalNotes.title: Not Every 800 Has GTIA
historicalNotes.text: Early Atari 800s used CTIA. GTIA entered new 400 and 800 machines in early 1982, adding three graphics modes. The 16-color game statistic uses the later factory GTIA capability, including 16 shades at 80×192; it is not the number of colors simultaneously available in the original high-resolution mode.

historicalNotes.title: A Family, Not Identical Machines
historicalNotes.text: The XL computers succeeded the 400 and 800 in 1983, followed by the XE range. They inherited much of the Atari software and SIO peripheral ecosystem, but operating-system revisions and RAM requirements can matter. Hardware expansions designed for XL or XE machines are not automatically suitable for the original 800.

overview:
The Atari 800 reached the market in late 1979 as Atari's expandable home computer, priced at about $999 in the United States. Unlike the lower-cost Atari 400, it had a full-travel keyboard, two cartridge slots, a monitor output, and accessible memory modules beneath its removable top. The left cartridge slot accepted the familiar Atari BASIC and game cartridges; relatively little software used the right slot.

Early configurations included 8 KB of RAM, with 16 KB versions also sold and expansion to 48 KB through plug-in modules. Later machines were supplied with 48 KB. Atari's 10 KB operating-system ROM did not include BASIC: the language occupied a separate 8 KB cartridge. SIO connected cassette recorders, disk drives, and other peripherals, while four controller ports supported joysticks and paddles.

ANTIC handled display lists and scrolling, POKEY supplied four-channel sound, and CTIA provided the original color-video circuitry. Later production used GTIA, adding modes such as 16 shades at 80×192; neither a 256-color screen nor GTIA was a universal launch specification. The XL and XE ranges continued much of the software ecosystem, though memory requirements and operating-system differences could affect compatibility.

historicalNotes.title: The Heathkit Experience
historicalNotes.text: Building a Heathkit was a rite of passage for electronics enthusiasts. The H89 kit came with Heathkit's famous assembly manuals - hundreds of pages of meticulous step-by-step instructions with detailed illustrations. Each wire, each solder connection was documented. Many owners recall the H89 build as one of the most rewarding projects they ever completed.

historicalNotes.title: Heath and Zenith
historicalNotes.text: Zenith Electronics acquired Heath Company in 1979. After the acquisition, the H89 was also sold pre-assembled as the Zenith Z-89 (and later the Z-90). Zenith's versions found their way into schools and businesses that wanted the machine without the kit-building experience. The Zenith badge helped legitimize the platform in corporate environments.

overview: The Heathkit H89, released in 1979 by the Heath Company of Benton Harbor, Michigan, was one of the most popular kit computers of the CP/M era. Also sold pre-assembled as the Zenith Z-89, it combined a Z80 processor, a built-in CRT terminal, and a floppy disk drive into an elegant all-in-one package. The H89 was a serious business and educational machine that ran CP/M, giving it access to a vast library of professional software including WordStar, dBASE, and Turbo Pascal. Heathkit's legendary assembly manuals - with their step-by-step instructions and detailed illustrations - made the H89 kit one of the most satisfying build experiences in computing history.

historicalNotes.title: Acorn's First Mass-Market Computer
historicalNotes.text: The Acorn Atom was the machine that put Acorn Computers on the map. Its success and the engineering expertise gained during its development directly led to Acorn winning the prestigious BBC Computer Literacy Project contract, resulting in the BBC Micro.

historicalNotes.title: A Modular Design Ahead of Its Time
historicalNotes.text: The Atom's motherboard was designed with expansion in mind, featuring internal sockets for add-on boards. The optional Colour Card plugged directly into the motherboard and added multi-colour graphics modes via a dedicated video circuit. RAM expansion boards could take the system from 2 KB to 12 KB using Acorn's own upgrades, or up to 32 KB with third-party boards. Additional ROM/EPROM sockets allowed users to add floating-point BASIC, toolkits, or custom firmware. This modular philosophy carried forward into the BBC Micro's legendary expansion bus.

photos.caption: Original advertisement for the Acorn Atom

overview:
The Acorn Atom, released in 1980, was Acorn Computers' first mass-market home computer and the direct predecessor to the BBC Micro. Powered by a MOS 6502 processor running at 1 MHz with just 2 KB of RAM (expandable to 12 KB), it offered surprisingly capable graphics for its time. The Atom featured a unique BASIC dialect called Atom BASIC that included inline assembler support. Sold as both a kit and assembled unit, it established Acorn's reputation for quality engineering and helped them win the BBC Computer Literacy Project contract.

The Atom was designed with expandability in mind. An optional Colour Card added multi-colour graphics output, transforming the default monochrome display into something more competitive with its contemporaries. RAM expansion boards could boost the Atom from its base 2 KB up to 12 KB or even 32 KB with third-party upgrades, and additional ROM/EPROM sockets allowed extra programming languages and utilities to be installed. Acorn also offered a floating-point controller card, parallel and serial I/O boards, and an external disk interface, making the Atom remarkably versatile for such an affordable machine.

historicalNotes.title: Overheating Disaster
historicalNotes.text: Steve Jobs insisted the Apple III have no cooling fan to maintain a silent, professional appearance. This decision proved catastrophic - chips literally worked loose from their sockets due to thermal expansion. Apple's official fix was to 'lift the computer six inches and drop it' to reseat the chips. The reliability crisis permanently damaged the Apple III's reputation.

historicalNotes.title: Designed by Committee
historicalNotes.text: Unlike the Apple II, which was Steve Wozniak's personal vision, the Apple III was designed by a marketing-driven committee. Engineers were given a list of required features and told to make them fit. The result was an over-engineered, overpriced machine that pleased neither business users nor Apple II loyalists.

overview: The Apple III (1980) was Apple's first attempt at a business computer. Synertek 6502A @ 2MHz, 128KB RAM (expandable to 256KB), 80-column text display, built-in 5.25" floppy drive. Priced $4,340-$7,800. Only ~65,000 sold. Designed by committee with Steve Jobs insisting on no cooling fan, causing chronic overheating and reliability problems. Apple II emulation mode was included but deliberately crippled to push business users to Apple III software. Despite a revised "Apple III Plus" in 1983, the damage was done.

historicalNotes.title: The Business PET
historicalNotes.text: The CBM 8032's 80-column display made it genuinely competitive with dedicated word-processing machines and minicomputer terminals. In the UK, it was a common sight in schools, banks, and small businesses throughout the early 1980s. Commodore's IEEE-488 peripheral ecosystem - dual floppy drives, dot-matrix and daisy-wheel printers - made it a credible turnkey business system at a fraction of the cost of an IBM mainframe terminal.

historicalNotes.title: Why 80 Columns Mattered
historicalNotes.text: The 8032's 80-column screen made it far better suited to word processing and business software than Commodore's earlier 40-column PET models.

historicalNotes.title: Before Commodore Went Mass-Market
historicalNotes.text: Machines like the 8032 helped Commodore establish itself in schools and small businesses before the company's focus shifted decisively toward the home market with the VIC-20 and C64.

overview: The Commodore CBM 8032, released in 1980, was the definitive business model of the PET line. Where the original PET 2001 offered a cramped 40-column display, the 8032 stepped up to a full 80-column screen on a built-in 12-inch green phosphor monitor - essential for spreadsheets and word processing. Powered by the same MOS 6502 at 1 MHz with 32 KB of RAM and BASIC 4.0 in ROM, it connected to Commodore's IEEE-488 peripheral bus for the CBM 8050 dual floppy drive and daisy-wheel printers. Rugged and reliable, the 8032 was a fixture in UK schools and small businesses well into the mid-1980s, and today remains a benchmark for Commodore's pre-C64 business ambitions.

historicalNotes.title: Built at Breakneck Speed
historicalNotes.text: The DAI began as a rush project for Texas Instruments UK, which wanted a PAL-capable computer. A tiny Belgian team built the prototype in just a few months, and legend says Concorde was used to get it to the United States on time.

historicalNotes.title: Ahead of Its Market
historicalNotes.text: The DAI paired unusually advanced graphics with a pre-compiling BASIC that turned programs into bytecode before running them. It was technically brilliant but commercially fragile, and the company collapsed before the machine could build a large software ecosystem.

photos.caption: The DAI Personal Computer on display in a museum collection

overview: The DAI Personal Computer, released in 1980 by Data Applications International of Belgium, was a remarkably advanced machine for its time. Originally designed for Texas Instruments UK, who wanted a PAL-compatible computer, the DAI was built in just three months by a team of three engineers - with the prototype famously delivered to TI USA via Concorde flight. Powered by an Intel 8080A at 2 MHz, the DAI featured a Thomson EF9369 graphics chip capable of 528×240 resolution in 4 colors or 352×260 in 16 colors - graphics modes that predated the Amiga's HAM mode. Its pre-compiling BASIC interpreter converted code to bytecode before execution, an approach that anticipated Java by over a decade. The AY-3-8910 provided stereo three-channel sound, and an optional AMD AM9511 math coprocessor could accelerate floating-point calculations. The machine even included a hardware random number generator. Despite its technical sophistication, the DAI was a commercial failure. DAI filed for bankruptcy on May 6, 1982, and production was continued by InData (a Prodata spin-off) until 1984. Only six commercially released games are known to exist. The DAI found a niche in television graphics production in the early 1980s and was considered by the Dutch Teleac broadcasting organization for teaching computing before the BBC Micro was chosen instead.

historicalNotes.title: The First Million-Seller
historicalNotes.text: The VIC-20 was the first computer to sell more than one million units, a milestone noted by the Computer History Museum. Commodore used Star Trek's William Shatner in television advertisements to pitch it as an affordable successor to the PET. At $299.95, it brought colour graphics and a real keyboard to households that couldn't afford an Apple II or Atari 800.

historicalNotes.title: VIC-20 Memory Expansion
historicalNotes.text: The VIC-20 shipped with just 5 KB of RAM (3.5 KB usable by BASIC), which was limiting even by 1981 standards. Commodore and third parties sold memory expansion cartridges in 3 KB, 8 KB, 16 KB, and 24 KB sizes that plugged into the cartridge port. Many games and programs required a specific expansion level - boxes were labelled 'Requires 16K expansion' - making memory upgrades essential purchases for serious VIC owners. The cartridge port also carried the full address bus, enabling hardware peripherals well beyond simple ROM software.

photos.caption: The VIC-20 at a desk - Commodore's first mass-market colour computer
Commodore VIC-20 advertisement featuring William Shatner

overview: The Commodore VIC-20, released in 1980, was the first computer of any kind to sell one million units. At $299, it brought color computing to the masses. It used the MOS 6502 processor and featured the VIC (Video Interface Chip) providing 16 colors and three-channel sound. Though its 5 KB of RAM (with only 3.5 KB available for BASIC) was limiting, its low price, built-in BASIC, and cartridge port made it an ideal entry-level machine. William Shatner's TV advertisements helped make it a household name.

historicalNotes.text: At £99.95 assembled or £79.95 as a kit, the ZX80 was the first computer sold in the UK for under £100. That price turned a computer from a specialist hobbyist purchase into something ordinary households could realistically aspire to own.
historicalNotes.title: Britain's First Sub-£100 Computer

historicalNotes.text: To save chips and hit its aggressive price, the ZX80 generated its video signal in software using the CPU itself. Whenever the machine was busy computing, the picture disappeared entirely - a famously odd compromise that Sinclair addressed in the ZX81.
historicalNotes.title: The Blank Screen Machine

historicalNotes.text: John Grant of Nine Tiles Ltd wrote the ZX80's integer BASIC interpreter between June and July 1979. The code was 5 KB, but had to fit a 4 KB ROM to keep costs down - the following month was spent cutting it to size, sacrificing commands like DATA, READ, and RESTORE. Sinclair never paid royalties; Nine Tiles was only paid when Amstrad later bought the rights to the ROM. Nine Tiles still owns the rights to the ZX80 and ZX81 ROMs to this day.
historicalNotes.title: Nine Tiles and the 4 KB BASIC

historicalNotes.text: The ZX80's thin case halves were vacuum-formed and notoriously prone to cracks, especially at the plastic rivets joining the two halves. The decorative 'go faster' stripes on top were not cooling holes, although some desperate users drilled their own. Later US-market models used injection moulding, making them more robust. The board was designed by Jim Westwood, the software by John Grant, and the case by John Pemberton.
historicalNotes.title: The Fragile Case

overview:
The Sinclair ZX80 was the first computer available in the United Kingdom for under £100. Designed by Jim Westwood and sold by Clive Sinclair's company, it introduced an entire generation to computing. Its stark white case and membrane keyboard became iconic. The ZX80 used a Zilog Z80A processor running at 3.25 MHz with just 1 KB of RAM and 4 KB of ROM containing a simple integer BASIC interpreter. The display would blank during computation due to the CPU handling both processing and video generation - a limitation addressed in its successor.

Sinclair supported ZX80 owners with a clever upgrade path: an 8 KB ROM chip that replaced the original Integer BASIC with the ZX81's Floating Point BASIC, adding SLOW mode (which eliminated the screen blanking problem), decimal numbers, and new commands. Combined with a RAM pack, this effectively transformed a ZX80 into a ZX81 at minimal cost. Third-party companies also offered replacement keyboards with proper keycaps, addressing the original membrane's fragility.

historicalNotes.text: In 1980, the BBC launched an ambitious project to introduce the nation to computing. After evaluating several candidates, they chose Acorn's design. The resulting TV series 'The Computer Programme' debuted in 1981 and its follow-ups, combined with the BBC Micro in schools, achieved remarkable penetration of computing education in the UK. The Computer History Museum notes that viewers could follow along at home on their own BBC Micros, and the machine's expandable design - with ports for cassette storage, serial interface, and networking - made it ideal for the purpose.
historicalNotes.title: The BBC Computer Literacy Project

historicalNotes.text: Acorn's work on the BBC Micro led Sophie Wilson and Steve Furber to design the Acorn RISC Machine (ARM) processor. Today, ARM-based chips power virtually every smartphone on Earth - a direct lineage from the BBC Micro project.
historicalNotes.title: Birth of ARM

historicalNotes.text: The BBC Micro community remains one of the most active in retro computing. The Stardot forums (stardot.org.uk) host thousands of members developing new games, demos, and hardware. Projects like b-em and JSBeeb (which lets you play BBC Micro games in a web browser) keep the platform accessible, while the Pi1MHz project bridges the BBC Micro's 1 MHz expansion bus to a Raspberry Pi, giving the vintage machine access to modern storage and processing. New commercial-quality games are still being released in the 2020s.
historicalNotes.title: Stardot and a Living Community

overview: The BBC Microcomputer, built by Acorn Computers for the BBC's Computer Literacy Project, became the educational computer of choice in British schools throughout the 1980s. Designed by Steve Furber and Sophie Wilson, it featured a fast 2 MHz 6502 processor, excellent BBC BASIC with a built-in assembler, and extensive I/O capabilities including the Tube interface for second processors. The BBC Micro was built to a high standard with a proper full-travel keyboard, and its expandability made it popular in education, business, and scientific applications. Acorn's work on the BBC Micro led directly to the development of the ARM processor. Thousands of BBC Micros were installed in UK schools through the 1980s and early 1990s, and for an entire generation of British children, it was their first experience of computing. The distinctive two-tone "bleep-boop" the machine makes when powered on is permanently etched into the subconscious of anyone who attended a British school in that era - and has been known to trigger mild PTSD in adults of a certain age.

historicalNotes.title: Notebook-Sized Computing
historicalNotes.text: Epson's HX-20 helped establish notebook-sized, battery-powered computing. Demonstrated in 1981 and released in 1982, it combined a keyboard, LCD, printer, and storage in an A4-sized package. Claims about the 'first laptop' depend on how laptops, pocket computers, and earlier portables are defined.

historicalNotes.title: Engineering Marvel
historicalNotes.text: Fitting a computer, printer, display, and cassette drive into a notebook-sized package in 1981 was a remarkable engineering achievement. Epson's expertise in miniaturization from their printer business proved invaluable. The dual-CPU architecture was clever: one processor ran user programs while the other handled I/O, display, and the printer independently.

photos.caption: The Epson HX-20 - a pioneering notebook-sized portable computer
The Epson HX-20 in its carrying case - truly portable computing in 1982

overview: The Epson HX-20, unveiled at the 1981 COMDEX show and shipped in 1982, is widely recognized as a pioneering A4-sized notebook computer. Weighing just 1.6 kg and running on rechargeable batteries, it packed a remarkable amount of technology into a notebook-sized package: a full-travel keyboard, a 4-line LCD screen, a built-in micro-cassette drive for storage, and even a tiny dot-matrix printer. Powered by dual Hitachi 6301 processors (one handling I/O), it ran Microsoft BASIC from ROM and could operate for up to 50 hours on a single charge. The HX-20 proved that portable computing was possible and paved the way for the laptop revolution that followed.

historicalNotes.title: Open Architecture Revolution
historicalNotes.text: IBM's decision to publish complete technical reference manuals - including BIOS source code - was revolutionary. This openness, intended to encourage third-party development, instead enabled competitors to create compatible 'clones.' IBM lost control of the standard it created, but the IBM PC architecture became the foundation of modern personal computing.

historicalNotes.title: The IBM Effect
historicalNotes.text: When IBM entered the personal computer market, it legitimized the entire industry overnight. Corporate purchasing departments that had dismissed Apple and Commodore machines suddenly had permission to buy personal computers - because they came from IBM. The phrase 'Nobody ever got fired for buying IBM' captured this transformation perfectly.

overview: The IBM Personal Computer Model 5150 (1981) transformed the personal computer from a hobbyist curiosity into a legitimate business tool. Intel 8088 @ 4.77MHz, 16KB RAM expandable to 256KB, PC DOS 1.0 (Microsoft's MS-DOS). Priced $1,565-$6,000 depending on configuration. Approximately 2 million sold. IBM's open architecture - publishing complete technical specifications - allowed third-party expansion cards and clones, inadvertently creating the "IBM compatible" standard that dominates personal computing to this day.

overview: The NEC PC-6001, released in 1981, was NEC's entry-level home computer designed to be more affordable and accessible than their professional PC-8801. Known affectionately as 'Papicom' (a portmanteau of 'personal' and 'computer'), it featured colorful graphics, three-channel sound, and an excellent implementation of BASIC. The PC-6001 was enormously popular in Japanese homes and schools, selling over a million units across its various models. It became many Japanese programmers' first computer and helped establish NEC's dominance in the Japanese computer market. Its success led to the improved PC-6001mkII and PC-6601 models.

overview: The NEC PC-8801, released in 1981, was one of the most important personal computers in Japanese computing history. overview: The Osborne 1 (1981) helped popularize portable computing with an integrated software bundle. Z80A @ 4MHz, 64KB RAM, tiny 5" CRT display, dual 5.25" floppy drives, running CP/M. Priced at $1,795 with $1,500 worth of bundled software including WordStar and SuperCalc. Approximately 125,000 units sold. Designed by Adam Osborne and Lee Felsenstein, it weighed 24.5 pounds and fit under an airline seat. The Osborne Computer Corporation's rapid rise and spectacular collapse became a cautionary tale in Silicon Valley history.

historicalNotes.title: The Peripheral Expansion System
historicalNotes.text: Texas Instruments designed the TI-99/4A around an external Peripheral Expansion Box - a large beige unit that connected via a side-port bus and could house up to eight expansion cards. Cards were available for disk drives (the Disk Memory System), RS-232 serial ports, 32 KB RAM expansion, speech synthesis, a modem, and even a Pascal compiler on a card. The system was more elegant than most competitors' approaches, but the PEB's price (around $500 for the box alone) put it beyond many home users.

historicalNotes.title: Speak & Spell's Big Brother
historicalNotes.text: Texas Instruments had deep roots in speech synthesis - their Speak & Spell educational toy used the same TMS5200 Linear Predictive Coding speech chip that appeared in the TI-99/4A's optional Speech Synthesizer peripheral. The Speech Synthesizer plugged into the side port and contained a vocabulary of around 250 words in a natural-sounding American English voice. It was used by a number of cartridge games and the built-in TI-Extended BASIC interpreter, and it remains one of the best-quality speech peripherals from the era.

overview: The Texas Instruments TI-99/4A was unique among home computers in using a true 16-bit processor - the TMS9900, originally designed for minicomputers. However, its architecture bottlenecked this powerful CPU with an 8-bit data bus and limited memory access. The machine featured excellent sprite-based graphics via the TMS9918A video chip, a full-stroke keyboard, and TI Extended BASIC available on cartridge. TI engaged in a brutal price war with Commodore in 1983, ultimately withdrawing from the home computer market after losing hundreds of millions of dollars.

historicalNotes.text: At under £50 as a kit, the ZX81 brought computing within reach of ordinary families. It was sold through high-street retailer WH Smith, making it the first computer many people ever saw in a shop.
historicalNotes.title: The £49.95 Revolution

historicalNotes.text: The infamous 16 KB RAM pack connected via a wobbly edge connector. A slight nudge would crash the machine, losing all work. Users devised creative solutions including Blu Tack, rubber bands, and eventually third-party replacement connectors. The problem was so widespread it became a cultural touchstone of early home computing.
historicalNotes.title: The RAM Pack Wobble

historicalNotes.text: The ZX81's open edge connector and its enormous installed base made it a magnet for third-party hardware developers. Dozens of small British companies sprang up to sell RAM packs, printer interfaces, sound cards, speech synthesisers, and full keyboards. Many were run from spare bedrooms and garden sheds, advertised in the back pages of magazines like Sinclair User and Your Computer. Some never amounted to much, but others grew into significant businesses - or gave their founders the engineering and entrepreneurial experience that launched later careers. The same pattern repeated even more vigorously with the ZX Spectrum, and the two machines together created a generation of British hardware entrepreneurs that had no real parallel anywhere else in the world.
historicalNotes.title: A Cottage Industry is Born

historicalNotes.text: Decades after production ended, new hardware for the ZX81 is still being designed and sold. The Chroma 81 interface adds colour to the monochrome display by mapping colour attributes to screen cells - a feat the original hardware could never manage. The ZXpand+ is a compact cartridge-style add-on providing 32 KB RAM, AY sound, a reset button, and SD card storage, replacing the unreliable edge-connector RAM pack entirely. Community projects have also produced fresh PCB re-runs of the original design, keeping the ZX81 alive as both a learning platform and a collector's item.
historicalNotes.title: Modern Hardware Revival

overview: The Sinclair ZX81, released in March 1981, improved upon the ZX80 with a new ROM containing a floating-point BASIC interpreter and a redesigned ULA chip that reduced the component count dramatically. Its striking minimalist case was designed by Rick Dickinson, whose industrial design won a British Design Council award. At just £69.95 assembled (or £49.95 as a kit), it became the first truly affordable home computer and sold over 1.5 million units worldwide. Its 1 KB of RAM was famously limiting - the 16 KB RAM pack that plugged into the rear expansion port became essential, though its wobbly connection was a constant source of frustration. The ZX81 sparked a bedroom coding revolution in the UK and established Sinclair as a household name.

historicalNotes.text: Jack Tramiel's aggressive pricing strategy at Commodore - 'We need to build computers for the masses, not the classes' - drove the C64's price from $595 to under $200. This price war contributed to the video game crash of 1983 and forced Texas Instruments out of the home computer market entirely.
historicalNotes.title: The Price War

historicalNotes.text: The Commodore 64 is recognized by the 2006 Guinness Book of World Records as the greatest-selling single computer model of all time. By the time it was discontinued in 1993 - over a decade after its 1982 launch - an estimated 22 million units had been sold worldwide. The Computer History Museum notes that its $595 price point, combined with 64 KB of RAM and impressive graphics, gave it a combination of capability and affordability that no rival could match at launch.
historicalNotes.title: 22 Million Sold

historicalNotes.text: Bob Yannes designed the SID 6581 sound chip wanting to build a real synthesizer on a chip. Its analog filters, ring modulation, and ADSR envelopes gave the C64 sound capabilities that inspired an entire music subculture. 'SID music' remains actively composed today, with new techniques still being discovered decades later.
historicalNotes.title: The SID Chip Legacy

historicalNotes.text: The C64 became the birthplace of the demo scene - programmers pushing the hardware far beyond its intended limits. Techniques like raster interrupts, sprite multiplexing, and undocumented opcodes produced visual effects that were thought to be impossible, and the tradition continues today.
historicalNotes.title: The Demo Scene

historicalNotes.text: In 2018, developer Gideon Zweijtzer released the Ultimate 64 - an FPGA-based C64 motherboard that fits inside an original C64 case. It faithfully recreates the SID, VIC-II, and CPU in logic, adds USB and Ethernet, supports multiple SID chips simultaneously, and includes the Ultimate 1541-II cartridge interface for disk image loading. It is one of the most sophisticated retro hardware revivals of any classic computer, preserving every quirk of the original silicon while adding conveniences that make the machine genuinely practical today.
historicalNotes.title: The Ultimate 64

historicalNotes.text: Beyond the major modern hardware projects, the C64 has a wealth of practical add-ons for everyday use. SysCheck cartridges combine 512 KB RAM expansion, diagnostic tools, and a quick-launch menu system in a single slot. S-Video and RGB upgrade kits recover the sharpness that composite connections lose, making a real difference on modern televisions. The Mega Multi Controller Adapter allows modern controllers and Sega Master System or Mega Drive gamepads to be used on the standard DB-9 joystick ports. Companies such as Monster Joysticks produce high-quality arcade-style sticks with autofire and two-button support, offering greater precision than the original Competition Pro.
historicalNotes.title: Practical Modern Add-Ons

overview:
The Commodore 64, released in August 1982 at $595, became the best-selling single personal computer model of all time with estimates of 12.5 to 17 million units sold. It combined the MOS 6510 CPU with 64 KB of RAM, the VIC-II graphics chip (320×200 resolution, 16 colors, hardware sprites, smooth scrolling), and the legendary SID 6581 sound synthesizer (three voices with ADSR envelopes, ring modulation, and a programmable filter). This combination of affordable price, capable hardware, and an enormous software library - over 10,000 commercial titles - made it the dominant home computer of the 1980s.

In 1984, Commodore released the SX-64 - a portable version of the C64 with a built-in 5-inch color CRT display and 1541 floppy disk drive, all packed into a luggable case weighing about 10 kg. It was the first full-color portable computer. Despite its hefty weight and price tag ($995), it found a niche with C64 enthusiasts who wanted to take their software on the road, and it remains a prized collector's item today.

historicalNotes.text: Built in Port Talbot, the Dragon 32 was part of a serious attempt to create a home-computer industry in South Wales. For a brief period it looked like a credible British alternative to Sinclair, Commodore, and the BBC Micro.

historicalNotes.text: Its Motorola 6809E was widely admired as one of the strongest 8-bit processors of the era, and Dragon BASIC made a good impression on reviewers. historicalNotes.text: After Dragon Data collapsed in 1984, the platform briefly lived on in Spain under Eurohard. Spanish-produced Dragons and the later Dragon 200 gave the machine a longer afterlife than many British buyers realized.

overview: The Dragon 32, manufactured by Dragon Data Ltd in Port Talbot, Wales, was based on the Tandy TRS-80 Color Computer architecture. While it was a capable machine, its limited graphics modes (semigraphics rather than true pixel-addressable modes) and small software library hampered its competitiveness. Dragon Data went into receivership in 1984.

historicalNotes.title: The Dual-CPU Innovation
historicalNotes.text: The FM-7's dual-CPU architecture was ahead of its time. By dedicating a separate 68B09 processor with its own 48 KB of RAM to graphics processing, Fujitsu created a system where the main CPU could continue computation while graphics were being drawn - a concept that foreshadowed modern GPU architectures.

historicalNotes.title: A Cheaper FM-8 Successor
historicalNotes.text: Released in 1982, the FM-7 was designed as a lower-cost, more home-oriented follow-up to Fujitsu's FM-8, bringing the company's 6809-based platform to a broader audience.

historicalNotes.title: An Important Game Machine
historicalNotes.text: The FM-7 became one of Japan's notable early game computers, hosting key titles and ports from companies such as Falcom, Game Arts, and Koei during the first half of the 1980s.

overview: The Fujitsu FM-7, released in 1982, was a technically innovative Japanese home computer notable for its unique dual-CPU architecture. It used two Motorola 68B09 processors - one for the main system running at 2 MHz and a separate sub-CPU dedicated to graphics processing with its own 48 KB of RAM. This design offloaded display rendering from the main CPU, resulting in smoother graphics performance. The FM-7 offered 640×200 resolution in 8 colors and came with 64 KB of main RAM. Priced at ¥126,000, it was more affordable than NEC's PC-8801 and competed strongly in the Japanese home market. The FM series evolved through the FM-77 and FM77AV before Fujitsu eventually moved to the more powerful FM Towns platform.

historicalNotes.title: The BBC That Wasn't
historicalNotes.text: The NewBrain was originally designed at Sinclair Radionics as a candidate for the BBC Computer Literacy Project. When the project moved to Acorn's design instead, the NewBrain was eventually manufactured by Grundy Business Systems. Its unique built-in VFD display allowed it to be used without a TV - unusual for home computers of the era.

historicalNotes.title: Model A vs Model AD
historicalNotes.text: The NewBrain shipped in two variants. The Model A was the cheaper version without the vacuum fluorescent display, relying entirely on a TV connection for output. The Model AD (A with Display) included the distinctive single-line VFD on top of the case, allowing users to type and debug BASIC programs without needing a television. The VFD showed 16 characters at a time and could scroll horizontally through longer lines.

historicalNotes.title: A Troubled Journey
historicalNotes.text: The NewBrain had one of the most tortuous development histories of any British computer. Conceived at Sinclair Radionics around 1978, it was originally meant to be Sinclair's next product after the MK14. When Sinclair Radionics collapsed, the design passed through the National Enterprise Board to Newbury Laboratories before finally reaching Grundy Business Systems. By the time it shipped in 1982, faster and cheaper competitors had overtaken it. Despite reasonable specifications, its late arrival and limited marketing meant sales never matched its potential.

overview: The Grundy NewBrain, released in 1982 by Grundy Business Systems, had a fascinating origin - it was originally designed by Clive Sinclair's team at Sinclair Radionics as a candidate for the BBC Computer Literacy Project. Powered by a Z80A processor at 4 MHz with 32 KB of RAM, it featured a unique built-in vacuum fluorescent display (VFD) that could show one line of text without a TV. The Model A shipped without the VFD, relying solely on a TV connection and selling for less. The Model AD included the distinctive one-line VFD on top of the case. Priced from £199 (Model A) to £233 (Model AD), it offered solid build quality and capable BASIC, but arrived too late to compete effectively with the ZX Spectrum and BBC Micro. Approximately 20,000 units were sold.

historicalNotes.title: The Jupiter Ace 4000
historicalNotes.text: Only around 800 Ace 4000 units were made for the US market, out of roughly 5,000 total Aces sold before Jupiter Cantab closed. The 4000 featured a stronger injection-moulded case (replacing the fragile vacuum-formed original), NTSC video, a channel 3/4 selector switch, a monitor output socket, and a ROM-deselect signal on the edge connector for external ROM boards. The speaker was moved to the bottom of the PCB with a case grill, allowing a larger heatsink. Surviving units are exceptionally rare.

historicalNotes.title: Why FORTH?
historicalNotes.text: Altwasser and Vickers chose FORTH because it was dramatically faster than interpreted BASIC - up to 10 times faster on the same hardware. FORTH compiled words into threaded code that ran close to machine-code speed, and its stack-based architecture needed very little RAM. For a machine with only 3 KB, this was a significant practical advantage. The name came from a special FORTH edition of BYTE magazine in August 1980, which had generated considerable interest. The downside was that FORTH's reverse Polish notation and stack-based thinking were unfamiliar to most home computer buyers, who expected BASIC.

historicalNotes.title: Named After a Pioneer
historicalNotes.text: The machine was named after the Pilot ACE (Automatic Computing Engine), one of the earliest British computers, built at the National Physical Laboratory in 1950. With 11 KB of storage, 32-microsecond cycle time, and a room full of valves and mercury delay lines, its remains are now in the Science Museum at South Kensington. Vickers and Altwasser's £89 Jupiter Ace fit in your hand and ran rings around it.

historicalNotes.title: From Spectrum to Jupiter Cantab
historicalNotes.text: Steve Vickers wrote the ZX Spectrum's ROM at Nine Tiles, while Richard Altwasser designed its hardware at Sinclair Research. After completing the Spectrum they left to start their own company, initially trading as 'Rainbow' - the name Altwasser had originally suggested Sinclair should call the Spectrum. When they discovered 'Rainbow' was already taken, they chose Jupiter Cantab - 'Cantab' being short for Cantabrigian, fitting since both held Cambridge degrees and had worked there with Sinclair.

historicalNotes.title: Boldfield's Second Life
historicalNotes.text: When Jupiter Cantab went into liquidation in 1984, Boldfield Computing Ltd acquired the machine, all remaining stock, and the FORTH rights. Boldfield commissioned new software including games, a database, and a spreadsheet, and introduced peripherals such as memory packs, monitor adapters, and a full-size keyboard. They sold everything by mail order but never manufactured new units, instead selling off parts for two years until stock ran out.

overview: The Jupiter Ace (1982) was a uniquely designed home computer created by Richard Altwasser and Steven Vickers, former Sinclair employees who had worked on the ZX Spectrum. Its most distinctive feature was using FORTH instead of BASIC as its built-in language. With just 3 KB of RAM and a Z80A processor, it was aimed at programmers who valued FORTH's speed and efficiency. A US variant, the Jupiter Ace 4000, was produced for the American market with NTSC video output and FCC compliance, but very few were sold stateside. Only around 8,000 Aces were made in total, making it one of the rarest British home computers.

Unlike the Osborne 1's tiny 5-inch screen, the KayPro II's 9-inch display was a genuine selling point. At $1,595 with a full software bundle, it offered remarkable value, and KayPro briefly became one of the best-selling computer brands in the US before the IBM PC clone market rendered CP/M obsolete.

historicalNotes.text: Kaypro's formula was simple but effective: bundle a large screen, dual drives, and serious CP/M software for less than many rivals charged for the hardware alone.
historicalNotes.title: Bundled Value Won Sales

historicalNotes.text: In 1983 and 1984, Kaypro was briefly one of America's best-selling computer brands before the market moved decisively toward MS-DOS and IBM compatibility.
historicalNotes.title: A Brief Sales Peak

overview: The KayPro II, released in 1982 by Non-Linear Systems of Del Mar, California, was one of the most successful CP/M portable computers of the early 1980s. Housed in an all-aluminium briefcase-style chassis, it included a built-in 9-inch green phosphor screen and two 5.25-inch floppy drives - making it a genuinely self-contained system. Running CP/M 2.2 on a Zilog Z80A at 2.5 MHz with 64 KB of RAM, it shipped with a generous bundle of software including WordStar, CalcStar, and dBASE II. At $1,595, it undercut the Osborne 1 while offering a larger screen and more software, and sold strongly until the IBM PC clone market made CP/M obsolete.

historicalNotes.text: The PC-9801's dominance in Japan lasted until the early 1990s, when IBM PC compatibles running DOS/V (a version of DOS with Japanese language support) began to erode NEC's monopoly. The final blow came with Windows 95, which standardized Japanese text handling on IBM-compatible hardware, ending the need for NEC's proprietary architecture.
historicalNotes.title: Japan's DOS/V Revolution

historicalNotes.text: The PC-9801 was home to thousands of exclusive games, many of which never left Japan. The platform was particularly important for the development of visual novels, strategy games, and RPGs. Titles like the Touhou Project, Policenauts, and countless others originated on PC-98 hardware.
historicalNotes.title: Gaming on the PC-98

overview: The NEC PC-9801, released in 1982, was the most dominant personal computer platform in Japanese history. Using a μPD8086 processor at 5 MHz with 128 KB of RAM, it offered 640×400 resolution in 8 colors - significantly higher than contemporary Western PCs. The PC-9801 ran its own version of MS-DOS and became the standard business and gaming computer in Japan for over a decade, maintaining a market share of over 50% through most of the 1980s and early 1990s. The platform was home to thousands of exclusive games, including many foundational Japanese RPGs, visual novels, and strategy games. NEC sold approximately 18 million PC-98 series machines before the platform was eventually displaced by IBM PC compatibles running Windows 95.

overview: The Sharp MZ-700, released in 1982, continued Sharp's unique "clean computer" philosophy - the machine had a monitor ROM but no built-in BASIC, loading languages and applications from storage. A cassette deck was built into the MZ-721 and MZ-731, but not the MZ-711. This approach allowed users to run different languages and operating systems. Using a Z80A CPU at 3.5 MHz with 64 KB of RAM, the MZ-700 offered 40×25 color text display and a built-in beeper for sound. Its most distinctive accessory was an optional plotter/printer that could produce color hardcopy output. Priced at ¥128,000, it was an affordable entry into Sharp's MZ series.

historicalNotes.title: Sord Computer Corporation
historicalNotes.text: Founded in 1970 by Takayoshi Shiina, Sord's name was derived from 'SOftware haRDware'. The company was a pioneer in Japanese computing before being acquired by Toshiba in 1985 - making the M5 one of the last computers to bear the Sord name.

historicalNotes.title: The Cartridge-Based BASIC System
historicalNotes.text: Unlike most home computers of its era, the M5 shipped with no built-in programming language. Users had to purchase separate BASIC cartridges: BASIC-I for simple integer programs, BASIC-G for graphics and sound (the most popular), and BASIC-F for serious floating-point computation. This unusual approach kept the base price low.

historicalNotes.title: M5 Pro and M5 Jr.
historicalNotes.text: The M5 Pro was not an upgraded model - it was actually a cost-reduced version with the same Z80A CPU and TMS9918 video chip but housed in a simpler, less expensive case aimed at the education and budget markets. The M5 Jr. was a console-only version without a keyboard, aimed purely at gaming.

historicalNotes.title: Korean Clones and International Variants
historicalNotes.text: In South Korea, three companies produced M5-compatible systems: LG's FC-150, Samsung's SPC-500, and Koryo Systems' TommyCom. All three added Hangul keyboard support. In the UK it was sold as the CGL M5, and in Japan, Takara marketed a version as the 'Game M5'. In many other countries it was sold as the 'Creative Computer'.

historicalNotes.title: The MSX Factor
historicalNotes.text: The M5's specifications - Z80A CPU, TMS9918 video, SN76489 sound - were remarkably similar to the upcoming MSX standard. When MSX machines arrived with backing from Microsoft, ASCII, and dozens of major manufacturers, the M5 couldn't compete with the ecosystem and was quietly discontinued.

overview: The Sord M5 (1982) was a Japanese home computer manufactured by Sord Computer Corporation - a firm founded in 1970 by Takayoshi Shiina, whose name derived from 'SOftware haRDware'. The machine used a Z80A processor at 3.58 MHz with the Texas Instruments TMS9918 video chip providing 256×192 resolution in 16 colours with 32 hardware sprites, and the SN76489 sound chip for three-channel audio plus a noise channel. With only 4 KB of RAM and 16 KB of VRAM, the machine was designed primarily as a games console - its BASIC interpreters were supplied on cartridges rather than built in: BASIC-I for integer arithmetic, BASIC-G for graphics and sound, and BASIC-F for floating-point math. BASIC-G was particularly impressive, with sprite handling, collision detection, and a powerful PLAY command for music composition. Contemporary reviews praised its speed, noting it was one of the fastest Z80A-based micros in its price range, with screen handling considerably faster than the Spectrum. In the UK it was sold by Computer Games Limited as the CGL M5 - initially at £195, later reduced to around £150. It was also marketed as the Sord M5 Creative Computer in many countries including Ireland, Spain, the Netherlands, and Australia, bundled with a carrying case. The M5 was reasonably popular in Czechoslovakia, where it was one of the first affordable computers available to the public. In South Korea, three companies produced compatible variants: LG's FC-150, Samsung's SPC-500, and Koryo Systems' TommyCom, all with Hangul keyboard support. In Japan, Takara sold it as the Game M5. Despite its short production run, the M5 attracted support from major Japanese game developers including Namco and Konami. Its specifications were very similar to the MSX standard, which likely forced the M5 out of the market by the mid-1980s. Sord Computer Corporation itself was acquired by Toshiba in 1985.

historicalNotes.title: The $99 Computer
historicalNotes.text: When the Timex Sinclair 1000 launched in July 1982, no computer had ever sold in the US for under $100. The $99.95 price point was a genuine cultural moment - Timex sold 600,000 units in the first year, and the machine was stocked in department stores and mail-order catalogues that had never sold computers before. It introduced computing to a vast swathe of American families who couldn't justify $600 for a Commodore 64 or $1,000 for an Apple II.

historicalNotes.title: Danny Ross and 171,000 Retail Locations
historicalNotes.text: Vice President Danny Ross, who had programmed FORTRAN in the 1960s, orchestrated one of the most audacious marketing campaigns in computing history. He leveraged Timex's existing retail network of over 171,000 locations - including K-Mart's 1,100+ stores, Macy's, jewellery stores, and drug stores - to sell the TS1000 in places that had never carried computers. His team achieved 28% market share, and the price eventually dropped as low as $19 during fierce competitive battles that reshaped the entire industry.

historicalNotes.title: A Thousand-Company Ecosystem
historicalNotes.text: By November 1982, Timex reported that 600 to 700 companies had sprung up offering add-ons for the TS1000. The community produced nearly 1,200 games, BASIC compilers, assemblers, and even implementations of Forth and Pascal. SYNC Magazine served as the flagship publication with over 6,000 subscribers, while Time Designs Magazine continued serving the community with 3,000+ subscribers long after Timex exited the market. Hardware hackers created full-size keyboards, sound synthesisers, and memory expansions up to 64 KB.

overview: The Timex Sinclair 1000, released in July 1982, was the American version of the Sinclair ZX81, manufactured under licence by Timex Corporation. It launched at $99.95 - the cheapest computer ever sold in the United States at the time - and promptly sold 600,000 units in its first year. The TS1000 was virtually identical to the ZX81, featuring a Zilog Z80A at 3.25 MHz, a membrane keyboard, and a monochrome display driven by software. Its 2 KB of RAM (double the ZX81's 1 KB) was still severely limiting, but the machine introduced hundreds of thousands of Americans to home computing at an unprecedented price. A 16 KB RAM pack was available for those who wanted to run larger programs.

historicalNotes.title: Bedroom Coders
historicalNotes.text: The Spectrum created a generation of self-taught programmers. Teenagers like Matthew Smith (Manic Miner), the Oliver Twins, and Rare's founders began their careers writing Spectrum games in their bedrooms, launching what would become a multi-billion pound industry.

historicalNotes.title: The Colour Clash
historicalNotes.text: The Spectrum's attribute-based colour system meant each 8×8 pixel block could only have two colours. Game developers devised ingenious workarounds, but the characteristic colour bleed when sprites moved became an endearing hallmark of Spectrum gaming.

historicalNotes.title: Loading from Tape
historicalNotes.text: Loading a game from cassette tape took 3-5 minutes, accompanied by distinctive screeching sounds. The loading screen would gradually appear in coloured stripes, building anticipation. Many games featured special loading screens that became artworks in their own right.

historicalNotes.title: A World of Peripherals
historicalNotes.text: The Spectrum spawned an enormous ecosystem of add-ons. Joystick interfaces were a cottage industry in themselves - the Kempston Interface became the de facto standard (its fire button on bit 0 of port 31), while Sinclair's own Interface 2 offered two joystick ports and ROM cartridge support. DK'Tronics sold a lightpen that worked with specially written software. The Currah µSpeech attached to the expansion port and used a Votrax SC-01 chip to add phoneme-based speech synthesis to Spectrum programs. Third-party memory expansions, RS-232 interfaces, printer adapters, and MIDI interfaces rounded out a hardware ecosystem that kept dozens of small UK companies busy throughout the 1980s.

historicalNotes.title: Modern Revivals
historicalNotes.text: The Spectrum name has been revived multiple times. 'The Spectrum' - a crowdfunded recreation developed by Elite Systems - aimed to bring the original experience to modern hardware, though its lengthy development attracted controversy. More technically ambitious is the ZX Spectrum Next, a reimagined Spectrum using an FPGA to replicate and extend the original hardware: it adds hardware sprites, a layer 2 320×256 graphics mode, AY sound, SD card storage, and enhanced Z80N instructions, while remaining fully compatible with the original 48K software catalogue. A second edition of the Next continues active development, with an enthusiastic community producing new games and demos.

historicalNotes.title: Rejected RAM Chips
historicalNotes.text: To save costs, Sinclair used rejected RAM chips for the 48K model's upper 32 KB of memory. These chips had been tested and found to have either a functioning lower or upper half of their original 64 Kbit capacity. A jumper wire on the motherboard selected which half to use (marked '3' or '4' for Texas Instruments chips, 'H' or 'L' for OKI), while a second jumper selected between the two chip brands since their bit cell geometries differed. This creative salvage of otherwise-rejected silicon was classic Sinclair cost engineering.

overview: The ZX Spectrum, launched in April 1982, was Sinclair's masterpiece and one of the most influential home computers ever made. Rick Dickinson's iconic rubber keyboard design - replacing hundreds of conventional keyboard components with just a handful of moving parts - and the rainbow stripe became cultural icons. With color graphics, sound, and up to 48 KB of RAM at an affordable price, it ignited the British home computing boom. Its vibrant software library - numbering over 24,000 titles - spawned a generation of bedroom programmers and game developers who would go on to shape the global games industry. The machine used attribute-based color, giving each 8×8 character cell a foreground and background color, leading to the characteristic "color clash" effect in games.
