historicalNotes.title: The Christmas That Never Was
historicalNotes.text: Acorn had enormous orders for the Electron in late 1983, with demand far outstripping what even optimistic projections had forecast. But Ferranti's custom ULA chip proved fiendishly difficult to manufacture - yield rates were dismal, and each batch produced far fewer working chips than expected. The Electron missed the 1983 Christmas market almost entirely. Retailers who had taken thousands of pre-orders were left empty-handed, and by the time supply normalised in spring 1984, many disappointed customers had bought a ZX Spectrum or Commodore 64 instead. The cash-flow crisis that followed nearly bankrupted Acorn, and the company was only saved by an investment from Olivetti in early 1985.

historicalNotes.title: The ULA Trade-Off
historicalNotes.text: The Electron's custom ULA was both its greatest strength and its Achilles' heel. By integrating virtually all of the BBC Micro's discrete logic into a single chip, Acorn slashed the component count and kept the retail price at £199. But the ULA had to share the same bus between the 6502 CPU and the video circuitry. In graphics modes, the CPU was halted every time the ULA needed to fetch screen data, effectively halving processor speed. Only in Mode 6 - a text-only mode that used far less memory bandwidth - could the CPU run at full speed. Clever programmers learned to exploit Mode 6 for computation-heavy tasks, switching to graphics modes only when needed.

historicalNotes.title: Third-Party Turbo Fixes
historicalNotes.text: The Electron's speed problems inspired ingenious third-party solutions. The Slogger Turbo Board added shadow RAM that sat outside the ULA's address space, so the CPU could access it without contention - effectively doubling speed in graphics modes. The Slogger Master RAM Board went further, adding 64 KB of sideways RAM and a turbo mode. These upgrades transformed the Electron from a sluggish BBC Micro clone into a genuinely capable machine, and are still sought after by collectors today.

historicalNotes.title: Elite on the Electron
historicalNotes.text: Ian Bell and David Braben's Elite - the legendary 3D space trading game - was ported to the Electron despite its limited hardware. The conversion required remarkable optimisation to run within the Electron's constrained memory and slower graphics modes, and it stands as a testament to what skilled programmers could achieve on the platform. The Electron version remained fully playable and delivered the same open-ended galaxy exploration that made Elite a classic.

historicalNotes.title: Modern Hardware Revival
historicalNotes.text: The Electron has a small but dedicated modern hardware scene. The ElkSD and similar SD card interfaces provide instant loading of the Electron's entire tape-based software library, replacing the agonising multi-minute cassette loads of the 1980s. Combined with composite-to-HDMI adapters and the original Plus 1 expansion, the Electron remains a charming and usable retro machine.

overview:
The Acorn Electron was a budget version of the BBC Micro, launched in 1983 at £199. It used the same 6502 processor and was largely software-compatible with its bigger sibling, running BBC BASIC and many BBC Micro programs. Acorn's strategy was to integrate most of the BBC Micro's discrete logic into a single custom ULA (Uncommitted Logic Array) chip, dramatically reducing component count and cost. However, this same ULA shared the system bus between the CPU and video circuitry, meaning the processor was halted during screen access in graphics modes - effectively halving performance compared to the BBC Micro in all but Mode 6 (text-only). The ULA also proved extremely difficult to manufacture. Ferranti, the sole supplier, struggled with yield rates, and production delays meant the Electron missed the crucial 1983 Christmas market entirely. By the time supply caught up in early 1984, the moment had passed and Acorn was left with a cash-flow crisis that nearly destroyed the company.

Despite these setbacks, the Electron built a loyal following. Third-party hardware like the Slogger Turbo Board and Master RAM Board worked around the ULA's memory contention by providing shadow RAM that the video circuit didn't need to access, dramatically improving performance. The machine ran an impressive software library including Elite, Chuckie Egg, Citadel, and Repton - games that proved the Electron was far more capable than its troubled launch suggested. Today, modern hardware like the ElkSD (and similar SD card interfaces) gives the Electron instant access to its entire software catalogue, and an active community continues to develop new games and utilities.

historicalNotes.title: The Enhanced Apple II
historicalNotes.text: The 'e' in Apple IIe stood for 'enhanced.' It reduced the Apple II+'s 100+ chips to a streamlined 31-chip design, making it cheaper to produce while adding features users had long requested - lowercase letters, a full ASCII keyboard, and 64 KB of RAM as standard.

historicalNotes.title: The Enhanced IIe
historicalNotes.text: In March 1985, Apple released the Enhanced Apple IIe - a revision that replaced the original 6502 CPU with the CMOS 65C02, upgraded the character generator to support the MouseText character set (for drawing GUI-like interfaces in text mode), and updated the system ROMs. Apple offered existing IIe owners an 'Enhancement Kit' containing the four replacement chips, which dealers could install for a modest fee. The Enhanced IIe became the baseline for later Apple II software.

historicalNotes.title: The Platinum IIe
historicalNotes.text: In January 1987, Apple introduced the Platinum Apple IIe - sometimes called the 'Advanced Apple IIe' - which repackaged the Enhanced IIe in a new platinum-grey case matching the Apple IIgs aesthetic. It included a built-in numeric keypad for the first time and came with the enhanced ROMs and 65C02 as standard. The Platinum IIe remained in production until November 1993, making the Apple IIe the longest-manufactured Apple computer in history.

historicalNotes.title: Apple's First GUI Computer
historicalNotes.text: The Lisa brought a mouse-driven graphical interface to Apple's product line a year before the Macintosh. Xerox's Alto and commercial Star system preceded it. Drawing on ideas demonstrated at Xerox PARC, Apple's team developed the Lisa's own document-centered desktop interface.

historicalNotes.title: A Beautiful Failure
historicalNotes.text: At $9,995 the Lisa was prohibitively expensive, and its Motorola 68000 CPU struggled to drive the GUI smoothly. Apple sold only about 10,000 units before discontinuing it. In 1989, Apple buried approximately 2,700 unsold Lisa computers in a landfill in Logan, Utah - a fate eerily similar to the Atari E.T. cartridge burial.

historicalNotes.title: Ambitious but Underfunded
historicalNotes.text: The Camputers Lynx offered impressive specifications - particularly its high-resolution display - at a competitive price, but the small Cambridge-based company lacked the marketing budget and production capacity to compete with Sinclair and Commodore. Camputers went into receivership in 1984.

historicalNotes.title: Troubled Early Production
historicalNotes.text: Early Lynx models drew criticism for not meeting published specifications and for manufacturing quality issues, which hurt the machine's reputation at exactly the moment a new platform needed developer confidence.

historicalNotes.title: Strong Hardware, Weak Timing
historicalNotes.text: Reviewers often liked the Lynx's keyboard and unusually sharp graphics, but technical merit was not enough in the crowded 1983-84 market. Camputers failed before the machine could build a large mainstream software catalogue.

overview: The Camputers Lynx, released in 1983, was an ambitious British home computer designed by John Shireff. Powered by a Z80A processor at 4 MHz with 48 KB of RAM, it boasted an unusually high-resolution display of 256×252 pixels with 8 colors - impressive for its price of £225. The Lynx featured a proper full-travel keyboard and a sophisticated BASIC interpreter. Despite its technical merits, Camputers was chronically underfunded and struggled with production and distribution, preventing the machine from achieving the success its hardware deserved. The company went into receivership in 1984.

historicalNotes.title: A Disastrous Launch
historicalNotes.text: The Coleco Adam's launch in 1983 was one of the most troubled in computing history. The built-in printer's electromagnetic pulse could erase data tapes stored nearby. Early units had failure rates as high as 50%. These problems, combined with missed holiday deadlines, led to massive retailer returns and ultimately contributed to Coleco's bankruptcy in 1988.

historicalNotes.title: Computer and Console in One Box
historicalNotes.text: Coleco announced ADAM at the 1983 Summer CES as a complete home computer that also doubled as a ColecoVision expansion module. Bundling a printer and high-speed tape drives, it leaned heavily on game compatibility to stand out in a crowded market.

historicalNotes.title: Crashing Into 1983
historicalNotes.text: The ADAM launched into the same 1983-84 market collapse that devastated the North American video-game business. With reliability already in question, Coleco had almost no room for a second chance.

photos.caption: The Coleco Adam with its built-in letter-quality printer - the printer was also the power supply

overview: The Coleco Adam, released in 1983, was an ambitious but ultimately disastrous attempt by toy and game company Coleco to enter the home computer market. Built around the ColecoVision game console architecture with a Z80A processor at 3.58 MHz and 80 KB of RAM, the Adam came as a complete package including a built-in daisy wheel printer and proprietary high-speed digital data cassette drives. At $725, it offered impressive specifications on paper. However, the launch was plagued by quality control issues - the electromagnetic pulse from the printer could erase data tapes stored nearby, and early units had high failure rates. These problems, combined with missed delivery deadlines and negative press, led to massive returns and contributed to Coleco's eventual bankruptcy.

historicalNotes.text: The Compaq Portable generated $111 million in its first year of sales - the greatest first-year revenue in American business history at the time. This proved that the market wanted IBM compatibility from multiple vendors, and that IBM's open architecture had created an industry standard beyond IBM's control.

overview: The Compaq Portable began shipping in 1983 as an early fully IBM PC-compatible portable. Intel 8088 @ 4.77MHz, 128KB RAM expandable to 640KB, built-in 9" monochrome CRT display, $3,590. Compaq reverse-engineered IBM's BIOS in a clean-room process to achieve 100% compatibility. Sold approximately 53,000 units in its first year, generating $111 million in revenue - at the time, the greatest first-year sales in American business history. It proved the IBM PC standard could exist independent of IBM.

overview: The Dragon 64, released in 1983 by Welsh company Dragon Data, was an improved version of the Dragon 32. It doubled the RAM to 64 KB and added a built-in RS-232 serial port for communications and printer connectivity. Like its predecessor, it used a Motorola 6809E processor running at 0.89 MHz and ran Microsoft Extended Color BASIC. The Dragon 64 was largely compatible with the Tandy TRS-80 Color Computer due to shared hardware design, giving it access to a wider software library. Despite its capabilities, Dragon Data went into receivership in 1984.

historicalNotes.text: The XT's bundled 10 MB Seagate ST-412 hard disk was a game-changer. While hard disks existed before, the XT made them standard in personal computers. PC DOS 2.0 added hierarchical directories to manage the relatively vast storage - concepts like subdirectories and paths that remain fundamental to computing today.
historicalNotes.title: The Hard Disk Revolution

historicalNotes.text: The XT's architecture established 640 KB as the maximum conventional memory for DOS, a limitation that would plague PC users throughout the 1980s and into the 1990s. Bill Gates supposedly said '640K ought to be enough for anybody' - a quote he denies making, but which perfectly captured the era's underestimation of future memory needs.
historicalNotes.title: The 640K Barrier

historicalNotes.text: The IBM PC and XT enjoy a remarkable renaissance thanks to modern microcontroller-based expansion cards. PicoMEM, built around the Raspberry Pi Pico (RP2040), plugs into an 8-bit ISA slot and provides EMS expanded memory, solid-state storage via microSD, and ROM emulation - replacing scarce and fragile vintage hard disks. PicoGUS uses the same RP2040 chip to emulate a Gravis Ultrasound wavetable sound card, bringing rich audio to machines that originally only had a PC speaker. The TexElec ISA IDE-to-SD adapter offers another storage solution using the XTIDE BIOS, while the open-source XTMax card (Teensy 4.1-based) provides up to 640 KB zero wait-state conventional RAM plus 4 MB EMS in a single slot. These projects, mostly open-source and costing a fraction of vintage originals, have made the PC/XT one of the most actively enhanced retro platforms today.
historicalNotes.title: A Thriving Modern Hardware Scene

overview: The IBM PC/XT (1983) was IBM's enhanced Personal Computer featuring the first hard disk in a mainstream PC. Intel 8088 @ 4.77MHz, 128KB RAM expandable to 640KB, 10MB Seagate ST-412 hard disk, 8 expansion slots. Priced at $4,995. The XT established the hard disk as a standard PC component and the 640KB RAM limit that would haunt DOS users for years. It also introduced the 8-bit ISA bus standard that became the backbone of PC expansion.

photos.caption: An MSX computer - the universal home computer standard backed by Microsoft and ASCII Corporation

overview: The MSX was a standardized home computer architecture created by Microsoft and ASCII Corporation in 1983. Rather than being a single machine, MSX was a specification that multiple manufacturers - including Sony, Panasonic, Philips, and Toshiba - could build to, ensuring software compatibility. Based on the Z80 CPU with the TMS9918 video chip and AY-3-8910 sound, MSX machines were enormously popular in Japan, South Korea, Brazil, and parts of Europe. The standard evolved through MSX2, MSX2+, and MSX turbo R, gaining improved graphics and sound with each generation. The MSX is notable as the platform family where Konami developed Metal Gear (on the MSX2) and many other classic games.

overview: The Matra Alice, released in 1983, was a French home computer produced by a partnership between Matra (a major French industrial conglomerate) and Hachette (the publishing giant). Its compact design, colorful rubber keyboard, and low price made it accessible to families, though its limited 4 KB of RAM and basic specifications meant it was quickly overtaken by more capable machines like the Thomson MO5 and Amstrad CPC.

overview: The Mattel Aquarius (1983) was a home computer produced by toy company Mattel Electronics. The Aquarius was notoriously limited even by 1983 standards - Mattel's own engineers reportedly called it "the system for the Seventies" despite being released in 1983. It lasted only four months on the market before Mattel pulled it, making it one of the shortest-lived computers in history.

Memotech positioned it as a premium product, but at £299 it faced stiff competition from the cheaper Spectrum and CPC. The company attempted to diversify into the business market with the MTX RS128 and FDX disk system, but insufficient capital and poor distribution left them unable to scale.
historicalNotes.title: Quality Over Quantity

historicalNotes.text: Memotech pursued an ambitious but ultimately fatal strategy: a deal to supply a Z80-based computer to Coleco in the US fell through, and the company entered receivership in 1985. Despite the closure, the MTX retains a loyal following among vintage computer enthusiasts, and modern hardware projects continue to extend the platform.
historicalNotes.title: Memotech's Fall

photos.caption: The Memotech MTX512 keyboard

overview: The Memotech MTX512, released in 1983 by Memotech Ltd of Oxford, was a well-engineered British home computer that earned admiration for its build quality at a time when most rivals used cost-cut keyboards. Powered by a Zilog Z80A at 4 MHz with 64 KB of RAM, it used the same TMS9929 video display processor found in the MSX standard, delivering 256×192 graphics with hardware sprites and 15 colours. Its SN76489A sound chip provided three tone channels and noise. Memotech BASIC was a capable interpreter, and an optional FDX disk system made the MTX a credible small-business machine. Despite its strong specifications, Memotech could not match the marketing muscle of Sinclair and Amstrad, and the company collapsed in 1985.

historicalNotes.text: The Oric-1 was created by the Tangerine team behind the Microtan 65, but marketed through the new Oric Products International brand as a direct challenger to the ZX Spectrum. It was one of the quickest attempts to turn a British hobbyist design team into a mass-market home computer company.
historicalNotes.title: From Tangerine to Oric

historicalNotes.text: The Oric-1 sold especially well in France, where it became one of 1983's best-known home computers. Its success came despite a famously buggy ROM and unpopular keyboard, problems that pushed Oric to release the Atmos quickly.
historicalNotes.title: A French Hit With Rough Edges

overview: The Oric-1, manufactured by Oric Products International and released in 1983, was a British home computer that achieved significant popularity in France. Designed by a team from Tangerine Computer Systems, it featured a 6502 CPU at 1 MHz, up to 48 KB of RAM, and an AY-3-8912 sound chip providing three-channel music. Its graphics capabilities included a 240×200 resolution display with a unique attribute-based colour system. The Oric-1 was succeeded by the Oric Atmos in 1984, which featured an improved keyboard and updated ROM, and the machine developed a strong following particularly in France where it outsold the ZX Spectrum.

historicalNotes.text: Spectravideo's founder Harry Fox approached Microsoft's Kazuhiko Nishi with the SV-328's design as the basis for a universal home computer standard. Nishi refined the architecture into the MSX specification, which was adopted by Sony, Panasonic, Philips, and dozens of other manufacturers. The SV-328 was almost but not quite MSX-compatible - its different I/O port assignments meant software needed modification to run on true MSX machines.
historicalNotes.title: MSX Origins

historicalNotes.text: Despite its role as the MSX ancestor, the Spectravideo 328 is largely forgotten in American computing history. It sold modestly in the US market, overshadowed by the Commodore 64 and Apple II. However, in the MSX community, the SV-328 is recognized as the machine that started it all - the design that launched a standard embraced by over 20 manufacturers worldwide.
historicalNotes.title: Overlooked Pioneer

overview: The Spectravideo SV-328 (1983) was a Z80-based home computer that played a crucial but often overlooked role in computing history as the direct precursor to the MSX standard. Z80A @ 3.58MHz, 80KB RAM (64KB main + 16KB VRAM), TMS9929A video chip providing 256×192 graphics with 16 colors and 32 sprites, AY-3-8910 sound chip with 3 channels. Priced at $299. While not MSX-compatible itself due to differing I/O ports, the SV-328's architecture was the blueprint from which the MSX specification was developed, making it the spiritual ancestor of millions of MSX computers sold worldwide.

The CoCo 2 benefited from Radio Shack's extensive retail network, making it readily accessible to consumers across America.

historicalNotes.text: Bill Gates personally wrote much of the Model 100's ROM software, including its BASIC interpreter. It is widely considered one of the last products that Gates coded by hand. He reportedly worked on the code during a vacation, staying up late to debug the firmware. The quality of the ROM software - compact, efficient, and remarkably bug-free - is a testament to his programming skill.
historicalNotes.title: Bill Gates' Last Code

historicalNotes.text: The Model 100 became the de facto standard computer for journalists and war correspondents throughout the 1980s. Its built-in modem allowed reporters to file stories from anywhere with a phone line, its TEXT editor was simple and reliable, and its exceptional battery life meant it could last through a full day of coverage. Many major news stories of the 1980s were written on a Model 100.
historicalNotes.title: The Journalist's Computer

historicalNotes.text: The Model 100 was actually designed and manufactured by Kyocera in Japan, then sold under different brands worldwide: as the TRS-80 Model 100 by Tandy/Radio Shack, the NEC PC-8201 by NEC, and the Olivetti M10 by Olivetti in Europe. The Kyocera KC-85 was the original Japanese version. This made it one of the first truly international portable computer designs.
historicalNotes.title: Kyocera's Global Design

photos.caption: The Tandy Model 100 - a pioneering notebook computer
The Tandy Model 100 preserved in a museum - still beloved by retrocomputing enthusiasts

overview: The TRS-80 Model 100 (1983) was one of the first true portable computers and a landmark in mobile computing history. Designed by Kyocera and sold by Tandy/Radio Shack, it featured an 8-line LCD display, a full-size keyboard, built-in 300-baud modem, and Microsoft BASIC in ROM. Bill Gates reportedly wrote much of the ROM software personally - one of the last products he coded by hand. Weighing just 3.5 lbs and running 20+ hours on 4 AA batteries, it became enormously popular with journalists, writers, and business travelers. With approximately 6 million units sold across all variants (including the NEC PC-8201 and Olivetti M10), it was one of the most successful portable computers of the early 1980s.

historicalNotes.text: Launched in 1983, the Model 4 combined Model III backward compatibility with a faster native mode and a proper 80-column business display.

historicalNotes.text: Many owners regarded the Model 4 as the high point of the TRS-80 family, but it arrived just as IBM PC compatibles were starting to dominate small-business buying decisions.

overview: The TRS-80 Model 4 (1983) was the last in the TRS-80 line of Z80-based computers. It could run in Model III compatibility mode or its native mode with 64-128 KB RAM and an 80×24 text display. Its most significant feature was the ability to run CP/M, giving access to a vast library of business software. The Model 4 represented Tandy's final push in the Z80 market before shifting focus to MS-DOS compatibles.

historicalNotes.text: The TS1500 solved the TS1000's most embarrassing problem - the wobbly 16 KB RAM pack - by building the memory in from the start. But by 1983, the Commodore 64 had been dramatically cut in price and the Atari 800XL offered 64 KB for under $200. The TS1500's ZX81-derived architecture, with its character-based display and membrane keyboard, could not compete. Timex discontinued the machine within a year and exited the US computer market entirely in 1984.
historicalNotes.title: Too Little, Too Late

historicalNotes.text: Every TS1500 ever sold was manufactured at Timex's factory in Quinta dos Medronheiros, Portugal - the same facility that later produced the TC-2068. Portugal's engineering team proposed using the ZX Spectrum's case and keyboard, a significant departure from Middlebury's original concept of a silver-painted TS1000 case. The Ferranti ULA was replaced with a 68-pin NCR custom logic chip that reduced power consumption, improved display quality, and lowered RF interference.
historicalNotes.title: Made in Portugal

historicalNotes.text: The National Education Corporation adopted the TS1500 for its Technical Literacy Series - a $295 educational kit containing the computer, a TS2020 cassette recorder, eleven tutorial booklets, and a briefcase. It was one of the few institutional uses of any Timex Sinclair machine and showed that the 1500's educational roots still had value even as the consumer market moved on.
historicalNotes.title: The NEC Literacy Briefcase

historicalNotes.text: Programmer Will Collum modified the TS1000 ROM to support the TS1510 cartridge player and fix existing Sinclair bugs, but inadvertently introduced three new ones: a LOAD failure that jumped to the middle of an instruction at address 03E5h, a cartridge check routine that could crash if RAM at address 2000h held a 1, and a memory reporting error that made very long programs (approximately 16 KB) appear to be out of memory even with a RAM pack installed.
historicalNotes.title: Three New ROM Bugs

photos.caption: The Timex Sinclair 1500 - the TS1000 with a real keyboard and 16 KB RAM
The TS1500's improved case design

overview: The Timex Sinclair 1500, announced May 17, 1983 and launched in September at $79.95, was designed to expand on the TS1000's base while correcting its worst problems: the membrane keyboard, RAM pack wobble, and tape reliability. Housed in a ZX Spectrum-style case with 40 full-movement keys (a proposal from the Timex Portugal engineering team), it carried 16 KB of built-in RAM on a redesigned circuit board. The Ferranti ULA was replaced by a custom 68-pin NCR logic chip that consumed less power, improved display quality, and reduced RF interference. Every unit was manufactured at Timex's factory in Portugal. Despite these improvements, the TS1500 arrived in a market that had moved on - the Commodore 64 and Atari 800XL offered vastly superior hardware at competitive prices, and contemporary press struggled to explain who needed a monochrome ZX81-derived machine in late 1983. Notable afterlives included the National Education Corporation's Technical Literacy Series and Parker Electronics' adaptation as an HVAC controller interface.

historicalNotes.text: The TS2068 improved on the ZX Spectrum in almost every measurable way - better sound, extra graphics modes, a cartridge slot, composite video - yet it couldn't run standard Spectrum software. This incompatibility was the machine's fatal flaw in the US, where there was no existing Spectrum software library to draw on. In Portugal, where Timex operated a manufacturing plant and where Spectrum software was already popular, the TC-2068 fared better and sold in reasonable numbers.
historicalNotes.title: Spectrum's American Cousin

historicalNotes.text: Before launching the TS2068, Timex showed the press the TS2000 - planned as two models, the TS2048 (16K) and TS2072 (48K), at $149.95 and $199.95. Developer David Ornstein revealed he had been using a prototype '8-15 hours a day' for ten months before launch. The final machine shipped as the TS2068 with a redesigned ROM featuring extended BASIC commands (STICK, SOUND, ON ERR, FREE, DELETE, RESET) and bank-switching hardware that could theoretically address up to 16 million bytes of memory.
historicalNotes.title: The TS2000 That Never Was

historicalNotes.text: Despite Timex abandoning the US market in 1984, the TS2068 attracted one of the most dedicated user communities of any short-lived computer. The Timex Sinclair Users Group kept publishing newsletters, and hardware hackers extended the machine with RAM expansions, disk interfaces, and even TCP/IP networking decades later. The community continues at timexsinclair.com, with active development of new hardware and software, regular Zoom meetings, and a YouTube channel documenting ongoing projects.
historicalNotes.title: A Community That Refused to Die

photos.caption: The Timex Sinclair 2068 - Timex's enhanced ZX Spectrum for the US market

overview: The Timex Sinclair 2068, released in November 1983 at $199.95, was Timex's bold attempt to build an enhanced ZX Spectrum for the American market. While superficially Spectrum-derived, the 2068 was a significantly different machine: its SCLD chip added extended graphics modes, a cartridge slot accepted ROM software, and the AY-3-8912 sound chip gave it genuine three-channel audio - something the standard Spectrum lacked. Unfortunately, the 2068 was not compatible with standard Spectrum software, stranding it without a software library just as the home computer market became brutally competitive. Timex withdrew from the US computer market in 1984. The machine found a second life in Portugal and Poland, where Timex licensed it as the TC-2068 and TC-2048. A devoted community continues to support the 2068 today - the Timex Sinclair Users forum at timexsinclair.com remains very active, with ongoing hardware projects, software releases, and technical discussion.

historicalNotes.text: Amstrad lacked its own distribution network across continental Europe, so the CPC range was sold under different brand names in different markets. In West Germany, Austria, and Switzerland it was sold as the Schneider CPC - Schneider-Rundfunkwerke AG handled distribution and even manufactured some units locally. In Spain the machines were marketed under the Indescomp brand (and informally as the Orion CPC). The hardware was identical; only the badges and documentation changed.
historicalNotes.title: Schneider, Orion, and the European CPC

historicalNotes.text: Spain levied a higher import tariff on computers with 64 KB of RAM or less - presumably to protect local industry by making cheap entry-level machines more expensive. This created a problem for the CPC 464, which had exactly 64 KB. Amstrad's solution was characteristically pragmatic: a non-functional RAM chip was added to the motherboard of Spanish-market machines, pushing the nominal RAM count above 64 KB on paper and moving the machine into the lower-tariff bracket. The extra chip did nothing electrically - the computer still had 64 KB of usable RAM - but it was enough to satisfy customs. It became one of the more colourful footnotes in 1980s computing history.
historicalNotes.title: The Spanish RAM Chip Trick

historicalNotes.text: DK'Tronics, one of the busiest third-party hardware makers for Sinclair machines, also produced popular add-ons for the CPC. Their lightpen let users draw and point directly on screen using software that mapped the CPC's beam-scan timing. Their speech synthesiser used a Votrax or similar phoneme chip to add voices to games and educational programs. Amstrad itself offered an official Speech Synthesiser - a small dongle fitting the CPC's expansion port - which was used by a number of commercial titles and educational software packages. These products reflected how the CPC's standard expansion bus made it straightforward to add capable peripherals.
historicalNotes.title: A Rich Peripherals Ecosystem

overview: The Amstrad CPC 464, launched in 1984, took a radically practical approach to home computing. Alan Sugar's Amstrad sold it as a complete package: computer with built-in cassette deck and a dedicated monitor (green screen or color), eliminating the compatibility problems that plagued competitors relying on domestic TVs. The Z80-based machine featured 64 KB of RAM, the AY-3-8912 sound chip with three channels, and a capable Locomotive BASIC. The CPC carved out significant market share in the UK, France, and Spain with its pragmatic "it just works" philosophy. Outside the UK it was sold under the Schneider brand in Germany, Austria, and Switzerland, and under the Orion brand in Spain and some other markets.

historicalNotes.title: Snow White Design Language
historicalNotes.text: The Apple IIc was the first Apple product to use the 'Snow White' design language created by Hartmut Esslinger's Frog Design firm. Its clean, horizontal lines, light gray color, and compact form factor set the aesthetic direction for all Apple products through the late 1980s, including the Macintosh and Apple IIGS.

historicalNotes.title: Compact vs. Macintosh
historicalNotes.text: The Apple IIc launched just two months after the original Macintosh in 1984, creating an internal rivalry at Apple. Steve Jobs championed the Macintosh while the Apple II division - still Wozniak's team at heart - produced the IIc. Despite the Mac's revolutionary GUI, the IIc outsold it initially thanks to the massive Apple II software library.

historicalNotes.title: The IIc Plus
historicalNotes.text: In 1988, Apple released the Apple IIc Plus, an updated model featuring a 3.5-inch floppy drive instead of the 5.25-inch, a faster 4 MHz 65C02 CPU, and a built-in power supply. However, by then the Apple II line was winding down in favor of the Macintosh, and the IIc Plus saw limited production.

photos.caption: The Apple IIc - Apple's first portable Apple II
The Apple IIc on a desk - compact and self-contained with a built-in floppy drive

overview: The Apple IIc (1984) was Apple's first compact and portable Apple II - the "c" stood for "compact." It packed a complete Apple IIe-compatible system into a sleek 7.5-pound case with a built-in 5.25" floppy drive, 128 KB RAM, and a 65C02 CPU running at 1.023 MHz. Designed as part of Apple's "Snow White" design language by Frog Design, the IIc featured a built-in keyboard, 80-column display support, two serial ports, and a mouse port - all without expansion slots. It could connect to an external monitor or the optional flat panel LCD display. Apple sold roughly 400,000 units in the first few months at $1,295. The IIc was later succeeded by the Apple IIc Plus (1988) with a 3.5" drive and faster 4 MHz CPU.

historicalNotes.title: 1984 Super Bowl Ad
historicalNotes.text: Apple's '1984' television commercial, directed by Ridley Scott and aired during Super Bowl XVIII, is considered one of the greatest advertisements ever made. It positioned the Macintosh as a tool of liberation against conformity - a bold statement that defined Apple's brand identity for decades.

historicalNotes.title: Desktop Publishing Revolution
historicalNotes.text: The combination of the Macintosh, Apple's LaserWriter printer (1985), and Aldus PageMaker software created the desktop publishing revolution. For the first time, individuals could produce professional-quality printed documents, fundamentally changing the publishing, design, and advertising industries.

historicalNotes.title: Modern Upgrades Keep Classic Macs Alive
historicalNotes.text: The compact Macintosh family has a thriving modern upgrade scene. BlueSCSI and SCSI2SD replace aging and unreliable SCSI hard drives with silent, reliable SD card storage, while the Floppy Emu from Big Mess o' Wires emulates both floppy drives and hard disks via the external disk port - essential for the 128K and 512K models that lack SCSI. Joe's Computer Museum (jcm-1.com) produces the MiniPerformer+, an open-source 68030 accelerator that clips directly onto the Mac Plus's 68000 CPU with no logic board modifications, giving it dramatically faster performance. The Mac ROM-inator II allows custom ROM images with improved networking support. Combined with active communities at 68kMLA.org and Macintosh Garden, these machines remain remarkably usable today.

photos.caption: Classic Macintosh computers on museum display - the machines that changed computing forever
The Macintosh Portable - Apple's first battery-powered Mac, weighing in at 16 pounds
Apple Macintosh advertisement introducing its graphical interface and mouse

overview: The Apple Macintosh, introduced on January 24, 1984, revolutionized personal computing with its graphical user interface, mouse-driven interaction, and "desktop metaphor." Powered by a Motorola 68000 CPU at 7.83 MHz with 128 KB of RAM, it featured a built-in 9-inch monochrome display showing crisp 512×342 bitmap graphics. Though initially criticized for limited RAM and no hard drive, the Macintosh's intuitive interface, bundled MacPaint and MacWrite applications, and PostScript-based LaserWriter printer created the desktop publishing revolution.

historicalNotes.title: Budget Misfire
historicalNotes.text: The Commodore 16 was designed to replace the VIC-20 as Commodore's entry-level computer, but at $99 it competed directly with the deeply-discounted Commodore 64, which offered four times the RAM, superior sound via the SID chip, and access to thousands of existing software titles. Many retailers simply steered budget-conscious customers toward the C64 instead.

historicalNotes.title: The 264 Series
historicalNotes.text: The C16 was part of Commodore's 264 series - a family that included the Plus/4 and the never-released Commodore 232. The series used the TED chip for video and sound, which offered more colors than the C64's VIC-II but lacked hardware sprites and had inferior sound capabilities. The entire 264 line was a commercial disappointment in the US market.

overview: The Commodore 16 (1984) was Commodore's budget home computer designed to compete in the sub-$100 market. MOS 7501 CPU @ 1.76MHz, 16KB RAM, 121 colors via the TED chip (same as Plus/4), $99 retail price. Part of Commodore's ill-fated 264 series alongside the Plus/4, the C16 was incompatible with the massively popular Commodore 64's software library. Despite its capable BASIC 3.5 with built-in graphics and sound commands, the C16 was overshadowed by its own sibling - the C64 - which offered more RAM, better sound, and a vast software library at a similar price point.

historicalNotes.text: The Plus/4 found an unexpected second life in Hungary, where its low cost and capable BASIC made it enormously popular. A thriving Hungarian software scene developed around it, producing games, demos, and utilities well into the 1990s.

overview: The Commodore Plus/4 (1984) was positioned as a business-oriented home computer, shipping with built-in productivity software including a word processor, spreadsheet, database, and graphing application. It used the MOS 7501/8501 CPU and the TED (Text Editing Device) chip which handled both video (121 colors) and basic sound (2 channels). Despite its capable hardware and built-in software suite, the Plus/4 was incompatible with the hugely popular C64's software library. It failed in the US market but found moderate success in Europe, particularly in Hungary where it developed a strong following.

historicalNotes.text: Though the PCjr was a commercial failure, its enhanced graphics and sound capabilities (the 'Tandy/PCjr' video and TI sound chip) were adopted by the Tandy 1000, which became one of the best-selling PC compatibles. Many DOS games of the late 1980s supported 'Tandy/PCjr' graphics as an enhanced display option.
historicalNotes.title: The PCjr's Unexpected Legacy

historicalNotes.text: IBM aimed the PCjr at home buyers, but its chiclet keyboard, limited expandability, and awkward add-on modules drew immediate criticism from reviewers and customers.
historicalNotes.title: IBM Misread the Home Market

historicalNotes.text: IBM cut the PCjr's price repeatedly, yet production ended after barely a year on the market, making it one of the company's most famous PC misfires.
historicalNotes.title: A Very Short Life

overview: The IBM PCjr, released in 1984, was IBM's ill-fated attempt to capture the home computer market. Based on the Intel 8088 at 4.77 MHz with 64 KB of RAM and enhanced CGA graphics supporting 16 colors, it featured a detachable wireless infrared keyboard - an innovative but poorly received feature due to its chiclet-style keys and unreliable connection. At $669 for the base model, it was expensive for a home computer yet too limited for business use. The PCjr was discontinued in 1985 after poor sales, but its enhanced graphics and sound capabilities influenced the highly successful Tandy 1000 series, which was explicitly designed to be PCjr-compatible.

historicalNotes.title: MSX With Philips Reach
historicalNotes.text: Philips was one of the biggest European names to back MSX, and the VG-8020 gave the standard real retail visibility outside Japan. In the Benelux countries especially, that mattered because Philips already had trusted consumer-electronics distribution.

historicalNotes.title: Betting on a Standard
historicalNotes.text: Unlike many home computers that locked users into one brand, the VG-8020 belonged to the MSX ecosystem, where software was meant to move across manufacturers. Philips helped prove that the Japanese-led standard could become a real European platform too.

overview: The Philips VG-8020, released in 1984, was Philips' entry into the MSX standard. As one of the largest electronics companies in the world, Philips brought significant manufacturing and distribution capabilities to the MSX ecosystem. The VG-8020 used the standard MSX specification: a Z80A processor at 3.58 MHz, 64 KB of RAM, TMS9918 video chip providing 256×192 resolution in 16 colors, and the AY-3-8910 sound chip. Priced at ƒ799 in the Netherlands, it was particularly popular in the Benelux countries and helped establish the MSX standard in Western Europe. historicalNotes.text: KC 85 machines were often distributed through schools, clubs, workplaces, and long waiting lists rather than normal Western-style retail channels. That scarcity helped create an unusually dedicated scene of users who expanded and modified the machines they could actually get.

overview: The Mühlhausen KC 85/2–85/4 family began in 1984 and was manufactured by VEB Mikroelektronik Mühlhausen in East Germany. Its U880 processor was a Z80-compatible design running at about 1.75 MHz. The KC 85/2 had 16 KB of main RAM and 16 KB of video RAM, with a 320×256 display supporting 16 foreground and 8 background colors with attribute restrictions. Later models expanded the memory and graphics capabilities. The family used cassette storage and a modular expansion system. These machines must not be confused with Robotron's incompatible KC 85/1 (Z9001) and KC 87 family.

historicalNotes.title: Linus Torvalds and the QL
historicalNotes.text: A young Linus Torvalds in Finland owned a Sinclair QL as his second computer after a Commodore VIC-20. He learned 68008 assembly programming on it and even wrote his own assembler. This early experience with the QL's Motorola 68008 processor influenced his later work creating the Linux kernel on a 386 PC.

historicalNotes.title: Quantum Leap or Stumble?
historicalNotes.text: Codenamed 'ZX83' internally (the name still visible on early motherboards) and described as 'Son of Spectrum' in a 1982 interview with Clive Sinclair, the QL was announced in January 1984 but didn't ship until months later. Early units were so rushed that the ROM had to be supplied on an external 'kludge' dongle. Despite featuring genuine multitasking years before mainstream PCs, these reliability issues fatally undermined market confidence. The board was designed by David Karlin, the firmware and OS by Tony Tebby, SuperBASIC by Jan Jones, and the case by Rick Dickinson.

historicalNotes.title: The Psion Office Bundle
historicalNotes.text: Every QL was intended to feel productive on day one thanks to Psion's bundled applications: Quill for word processing, Abacus for spreadsheets, Easel for business graphics, and Archive for databases. This unusually generous software bundle gave the machine a serious small-business flavour and later evolved into Psion Xchange.

historicalNotes.title: Why the 'Kludge' Existed
historicalNotes.text: The notorious external ROM 'kludge' was not just a bug fix but a hardware workaround for a rushed launch. Sinclair had originally planned for 32 KB of ROM, then discovered the finished QDOS and SuperBASIC needed 48 KB, so part of the firmware had to live in a 16 KB external ROM cartridge until the motherboard was revised to hold the full ROM set internally.

historicalNotes.title: QDOS Lived On
historicalNotes.text: Tony Tebby's QDOS outlasted the original Sinclair machine by decades. It was reworked and extended into systems such as Minerva and especially SMSQ/E, which remains actively maintained by volunteers and still runs on advanced QL-compatible hardware and emulators.

historicalNotes.title: From Thor to Q40 and Q60
historicalNotes.text: The QL inspired a whole line of successors and compatibles after Sinclair abandoned it. CST's Thor machines in 1986 effectively packaged a QL into a more professional form with built-in drives and expansion, while the later Q40 and Q60 systems carried the same software lineage into the 68040 and 68060 era as spiritual descendants of the original concept.

historicalNotes.title: A Thriving Emulator Ecosystem
historicalNotes.text: The QL community produced an unusually rich family of emulators spanning multiple platforms. QPC2 (originally commercial, made freeware in 2016) ran SMSQ/E natively on Windows and was considered the best software emulator. Q-emuLator brought the QL to Mac and Windows, while QLay provided a free option for DOS and Linux. There were even hardware solutions: the QXL ISA card gave PCs a real 68040-based QL, and the ST-QL emulator ran QDOS on Atari ST hardware. RWAP Software and Dilwyn Jones assembled comprehensive archives of these tools, keeping the QL accessible to new users decades after production ended.

photos.caption: The Sinclair QL keyboard - controversial flat keys on Sinclair's business computer
In this TV advert, Sir Clive Sinclair literally leaps over the competing computers.

overview:
The Sinclair QL (Quantum Leap), launched in January 1984, was Sinclair Research's ambitious attempt at a professional computer. Its case was again designed by Rick Dickinson, earning an Italian Smau Industrial Design Award. Built around the Motorola 68008 processor running at 7.5 MHz with 128 KB of RAM, it featured the multitasking QDOS operating system and the powerful SuperBASIC programming language. The QL used innovative but unreliable Microdrives for storage. Notably, a young Linus Torvalds owned a Sinclair QL as his second computer (after a Commodore VIC-20), learning 68008 assembly on it before eventually creating Linux. Despite selling approximately 150,000 units, the QL was plagued by early reliability issues and missed its market window.

Its bundled Psion office suite - Quill, Abacus, Easel, and Archive - made it unusually useful straight out of the box, and the machine was widely seen as one of the first affordable 32-bit home computers thanks to the 68008's 32-bit architecture despite its 8-bit external bus. The QDOS line also lived on far beyond Sinclair itself through Minerva and especially SMSQ/E, which is still maintained by the QL community today.

historicalNotes.text: When IBM's PCjr flopped in 1984 due to its infamous chiclet keyboard and limited expandability, the Tandy 1000 swooped in with a proper keyboard, expansion slots, and full PCjr compatibility - all at a lower price. Many games designed for the PCjr's enhanced graphics and sound found their true audience on the Tandy 1000, making 'Tandy compatible' a standard feature listed on game boxes throughout the 1980s.

historicalNotes.title: Radio Shack Advantage
historicalNotes.text: Like the TRS-80 before it, the Tandy 1000 benefited enormously from being sold through Radio Shack's nationwide chain of stores. At a time when buying a computer often meant visiting a specialty dealer, Radio Shack put the Tandy 1000 in thousands of convenient locations across America.

overview: The Tandy 1000 (1984) was Tandy Corporation's IBM PCjr-compatible computer that succeeded where IBM's own PCjr failed. Intel 8088 @ 4.77MHz, 128KB RAM expandable to 640KB, SN76496 3-voice sound chip, enhanced CGA-compatible graphics. Priced at $1,199. The Tandy 1000 series improved on the PCjr's design while maintaining compatibility with its enhanced graphics and sound standards (later called "Tandy graphics"). Sold through Radio Shack stores, it became one of the best-selling IBM compatibles for home use throughout the mid-1980s.

historicalNotes.title: A Quality Alternative
historicalNotes.text: The Tatung Einstein earned respect for its build quality and capable specifications at a competitive price. Its inclusion of a built-in floppy drive when most competitors relied on cassette tape gave it an advantage in educational and small business markets.

historicalNotes.title: The Developer's Machine
historicalNotes.text: The Einstein gained a second, less-publicised role as a development and test platform for software targeting other 8-bit micros. Its full-travel keyboard, built-in floppy drive, and programmable Z80 CPU made it convenient for cross-developing and testing code destined for the Spectrum, Amstrad CPC, or MSX machines, without wearing out the target hardware. Small software houses and bedroom developers appreciated having a robust, floppy-based machine to write and test on.

overview: The Tatung Einstein, released in 1984 by the UK subsidiary of Taiwanese electronics company Tatung, was a well-built Z80A-based computer initially priced at £499 in the UK. Running at 4 MHz with 64 KB of RAM, it featured a TMS9918 video display processor for sprites and smooth scrolling, an AY-3-8910 sound chip for three-channel audio, and a built-in 3-inch floppy disk drive. The Einstein offered impressive specifications for its price and was popular in education, though it struggled to compete with the established ZX Spectrum and BBC Micro for home use.

historicalNotes.title: Plan Informatique pour Tous
historicalNotes.text: In 1985, the French government launched the Plan Informatique pour Tous, an ambitious program to place computers in every school in France. Thomson was chosen as a primary supplier, and the MO5 became the classroom machine many French students first encountered.

historicalNotes.title: Built for the Classroom
historicalNotes.text: The MO5's rubber keyboard and BASIC 1.0 in ROM reflected its educational role more than a luxury home-computing image. It was durable, easy to deploy, and distinctly French in a market often dominated by British and American machines.

overview: The Thomson MO5 (1984) was a French home computer manufactured by Thomson SA, featuring a Motorola 6809E processor running at 1 MHz, 48 KB of RAM, and 16 KB of ROM containing Thomson BASIC. It offered a 320×200 resolution display with 16 colors and basic 1-bit DAC sound output. The MO5 became hugely significant in French computing history as the primary computer chosen for the government's ambitious Plan Informatique pour Tous (IT for All Plan) in 1985, which aimed to place computers in every French school. At 2,790 FF (approximately $350), it was affordable for institutions, and over 100,000 units were deployed in French classrooms, making it one of the most widely used educational computers in European history.

historicalNotes.text: Under the case, the Spectrum+ was still basically a 48K Spectrum, but its larger keyboard and smarter styling made it look much more respectable in a shop window. historicalNotes.title: Upgrade, Don't Replace
historicalNotes.text: Sinclair even sold conversion kits so existing owners could transplant their old Spectrum into the new shell. It was a characteristically pragmatic idea: cheaper than a whole new machine, and perfect for a market full of handy teenagers with screwdrivers.

overview: The ZX Spectrum+ (1984) was an upgraded version of the 48K Spectrum featuring an improved injection-molded keyboard with a more professional feel, replacing the controversial rubber keys. Internally identical to the 48K Spectrum, its main improvement was the QL-style keyboard with a proper space bar and reset button. In a characteristically canny move, Sinclair offered existing Spectrum owners the new case and keyboard as a DIY upgrade kit for just £20, or £30 if you wanted Sinclair to do the conversion for you - letting loyal customers modernise their machines without buying a whole new computer.

historicalNotes.title: Schneider, Orion, and the European CPC
historicalNotes.text: Amstrad lacked its own distribution network across continental Europe, so the CPC range was sold under different brand names in different markets. In West Germany, Austria, and Switzerland it was sold as the Schneider CPC - Schneider-Rundfunkwerke AG handled distribution and even manufactured some units locally. In Spain the machines were marketed under the Indescomp brand (and informally as the Orion CPC). The hardware was identical; only the badges and documentation changed.

historicalNotes.title: The Spanish RAM Chip Trick
historicalNotes.text: Spain levied a higher import tariff on computers with 64 KB of RAM or less - presumably to protect local industry by making cheap entry-level machines more expensive. This created a problem for the CPC 464, which had exactly 64 KB. Amstrad's solution was characteristically pragmatic: a non-functional RAM chip was added to the motherboard of Spanish-market machines, pushing the nominal RAM count above 64 KB on paper and moving the machine into the lower-tariff bracket. The extra chip did nothing electrically - the computer still had 64 KB of usable RAM - but it was enough to satisfy customs. It became one of the more colourful footnotes in 1980s computing history.

historicalNotes.title: A Rich Peripherals Ecosystem
historicalNotes.text: DK'Tronics, one of the busiest third-party hardware makers for Sinclair machines, also produced popular add-ons for the CPC. Their lightpen let users draw and point directly on screen using software that mapped the CPC's beam-scan timing. Their speech synthesiser used a Votrax or similar phoneme chip to add voices to games and educational programs. Amstrad itself offered an official Speech Synthesiser - a small dongle fitting the CPC's expansion port - which was used by a number of commercial titles and educational software packages. These products reflected how the CPC's standard expansion bus made it straightforward to add capable peripherals.

Like the rest of the range it was sold as the Schneider CPC 6128 in German-speaking markets.

historicalNotes.text: Amstrad sold the PCW as a complete writing system - screen, printer, disks, and LocoScript - at a price that undercut many dedicated word processors and even challenged electric typewriters. It found homes in small businesses, schools, clubs, and spare bedrooms all across Britain and Europe.
historicalNotes.title: The Typewriter Killer

historicalNotes.text: Many buyers never thought of the PCW as a 'computer' at all, which was exactly the point. Alan Sugar marketed it as a practical office tool for people who wanted letters and invoices, not command prompts and technical mystique.
historicalNotes.title: A Computer Disguised as an Appliance

historicalNotes.text: Behind the appliance-style branding, the PCW was also a capable CP/M machine. Owners soon discovered they could run databases, spreadsheets, programming tools, and desktop-publishing software on the same hardware.
historicalNotes.title: The Hidden CP/M Workhorse

overview: The Amstrad PCW 8256 (1985) was a dedicated word processing system that became one of the most successful computers ever made, selling over 8 million units across all models. It included a Z80A processor, 256 KB RAM, built-in 3-inch floppy, dot-matrix printer, and the LocoScript word processing software. It was designed to be an affordable alternative to typewriters and was used extensively in offices and homes across Europe. An upgraded PCW 8512 variant followed shortly after, doubling the RAM to 512 KB and adding a second floppy drive.

historicalNotes.title: The XE Family
historicalNotes.text: The 130XE was the flagship of Atari Corp's XE range - the successor to the XL line. Its siblings were the 65XE (64 KB, sold primarily in Europe as a budget model) and the 800XE (64 KB, aimed at Eastern European markets). In 1987, Atari also released the XEGS, a game-console variant of the 65XE with a detachable keyboard, in an attempt to compete with the NES. All XE models shared the same ANTIC/GTIA/POKEY chips and ran the entire Atari 8-bit software catalogue.

historicalNotes.title: Twilight of the 8-Bit Era
historicalNotes.text: The 130XE represented Jack Tramiel's strategy to sell the existing Atari 8-bit technology at rock-bottom prices while investing in the new 16-bit ST line. At $149.95, it was one of the most affordable computers on the market in 1985, giving budget-conscious consumers access to the Atari 8-bit software library that included thousands of titles.

historicalNotes.title: Modern Add-Ons Extend the Platform
historicalNotes.text: Like all Atari 8-bit machines, the 130XE benefits from the modern hardware scene centred on the SIO bus. FujiNet gives the 130XE Wi-Fi connectivity, virtual drives, and full network access from a single SIO-connected device. The UNO Cart loads the entire Atari 8-bit software catalogue from a single SD card in the cartridge slot. SIO2SD provides affordable floppy disk emulation. The SIDE3 cartridge adds hard-disk capacity, and the Turbo 816 upgrades the CPU to a 16-bit 65816 for a significant speed boost. The Incognito board - designed specifically for the 800 but illustrative of the upgrade culture - provides 1 MB of RAM and an enhanced OS, and S-Video output kits deliver clean picture quality on contemporary televisions.

photos.caption: The Atari XE Game System - a console-style member of Atari's 8-bit XE family

overview: The Atari 130XE, released in 1985, was the flagship of Atari Corp's XE range - the successor to the XL line - introduced under Jack Tramiel's new management. Using the same 6502C processor at 1.79 MHz and ANTIC/GTIA custom chips as its predecessors, it offered 128 KB of RAM (bank-switched, with 64 KB accessible at a time) in a sleek new case design. The XE range also included the 65XE (64 KB, European budget model) and the 800XE (64 KB, for Eastern European markets). The 130XE maintained full compatibility with the massive Atari 8-bit software library while offering more memory for programming. At $149.95, it was one of the most affordable computers available in 1985, representing the twilight of Atari's 8-bit era.

historicalNotes.title: The Musicians' Computer
historicalNotes.text: The Atari ST's built-in MIDI ports made it the computer of choice for musicians throughout the late 1980s and early 1990s. Professional music software like Cubase and Notator (later Logic) was developed first for the ST. Many hit records of the era were produced using Atari ST-based studio setups, and some studios continued using STs well into the 2000s.

historicalNotes.title: The Jackintosh
historicalNotes.text: Nicknamed the 'Jackintosh' after Atari's new owner Jack Tramiel (former Commodore CEO), the ST brought affordable 16/32-bit computing to consumers in 1985. Its GEM desktop from Digital Research offered a graphical interface at a fraction of the Macintosh's price, making it popular for desktop publishing in Europe with Calamus and PageStream. The earlier Sinclair QL used the related 68008: a 16/32-bit processor with an 8-bit external data bus, not an 8-bit CPU.

overview: The Atari ST, released in 1985, was Jack Tramiel's first computer after acquiring Atari from Warner Communications. Nicknamed the 'Jackintosh' for offering a Macintosh-like GUI (GEM) at a fraction of the price, the ST used a Motorola MC68000 at 8 MHz with 512 KB to 1 MB of RAM. Its 640×400 monochrome mode was excellent for desktop publishing, while the 320×200 16-color mode served gaming well. The ST's most distinctive feature was its built-in MIDI ports, which made it the dominant computer in professional music production throughout the late 1980s. At $799 with a monochrome monitor, it dramatically undercut the Macintosh and found success in Europe, particularly in the UK, Germany, and France.

historicalNotes.text: The Commodore 128 could boot into native C128 mode, a near-complete Commodore 64 mode, or CP/M using its built-in Z80 processor. That made it one of the most flexible 8-bit-era machines ever sold - a bridge between home gaming, serious productivity, and the huge existing C64 software library.
historicalNotes.title: Three Computers in One

historicalNotes.text: Unlike the C64, the C128 included a dedicated video display controller for an 80-column RGB text display, aimed squarely at productivity software and business users. In practice, that crisp 80-column screen made word processing, spreadsheets, and CP/M applications feel far more professional than on a typical home computer.
historicalNotes.title: The 80-Column Upgrade

historicalNotes.text: Bil Herd led the rapid design of the C128 under intense pressure inside Commodore, producing a remarkably ambitious machine in a short time. Yet because it arrived after the Commodore 64 had already become a cultural phenomenon, the C128 spent most of its life in the C64's shadow - respected by enthusiasts, but rarely loved by the broader market in the same way.
historicalNotes.title: Bil Herd's Shadowed Success

photos.caption: The Commodore 128 - the C64's successor with CP/M compatibility and 80-column display

overview: The Commodore 128, released in 1985, was designed as a fully backward-compatible successor to the Commodore 64. It featured three operating modes: C128 mode with 128 KB RAM and an enhanced BASIC 7.0, C64 mode for full compatibility with the massive C64 software library, and CP/M mode using a built-in Z80 processor. The C128 included a separate VDC chip (MOS 8563) providing an 80-column text display, making it capable as a business machine. While technically superior to the C64, most owners used it primarily in C64 mode.

historicalNotes.title: Lincoln Center Launch
historicalNotes.text: The Amiga 1000 was announced at a major event at New York's Lincoln Center in July 1985, featuring celebrities like Andy Warhol and Debbie Harry of Blondie. Warhol used an Amiga to create digital portraits of Harry live on stage - an extraordinary demonstration of the machine's graphics capabilities. The Computer History Museum notes the Amiga had audio and video capabilities beyond those found in most other personal computers of the era.

historicalNotes.title: The Amiga Lives On
historicalNotes.text: The Amiga platform has an unusually active modern hardware scene for a computer that last shipped new from Commodore in 1994. TheA500 Mini, produced under licence by Retro Games Ltd, is the most widely available option - a compact plug-and-play device running pre-installed games for the A500, A1200, CD32, and other models. AmigaKit's A600GS (2024) goes further, offering 2 GB RAM, 64 GB storage, HDMI, Ethernet, and USB in a small box with classic DB-9 ports for original mice and joysticks; it ships with Amibench, OctaMED, and PPaint alongside games. For the hardware-focused enthusiast, the MiniMig uses FPGA logic to recreate the Amiga chipset without emulation. Apollo's Standalone V4+ and the newer A6000 push performance far beyond anything Commodore produced, with the A6000 featuring 2 GB Fast RAM, 12 MB Chip RAM, HDMI output, 100 Mbit Ethernet, and a custom SAGA graphics core. A full-size THEA1200 - with working keyboard, USB ports, controller, and mouse - was previewed by Retro Games Ltd at Gamescom 2025.

photos.caption: The Amiga keyboard - a full-size layout worthy of a professional machine
The original Amiga 1000 launch - Commodore's groundbreaking multimedia computer

overview: The Commodore Amiga 1000, released in July 1985, was a quantum leap in home computing. Designed by Jay Miner and the team at Amiga Corporation, its custom chipset - Agnus (DMA controller), Denise (graphics), and Paula (sound/I/O) - delivered capabilities that wouldn't be matched by competitors for years. It offered 4096 colors, hardware blitter and copper co-processors, four-channel stereo PCM audio, and true preemptive multitasking with the AmigaOS. The Amiga became the platform of choice for video production, 3D animation, music creation, and gaming, and was used in broadcast television worldwide for graphics and special effects.

historicalNotes.title: Designed in Budapest, Aimed West
historicalNotes.text: The Enterprise was designed in Britain and later developed a particularly strong following in Hungary. Its custom Nick and Dave chips gave it advanced graphics and sound capabilities for an 8-bit machine.

historicalNotes.title: Too Late to Win
historicalNotes.text: The project was announced early enough to sound revolutionary, but delays meant it arrived into a market that had largely settled around other machines. By the time it shipped, its advanced design was still admired, but its commercial moment had passed.

overview: The Enterprise, released in 1985, was a British-designed computer that later found a strong following in Hungary. Using a Z80A processor at 4 MHz with 64 or 128 KB of RAM, it featured advanced graphics for its class: up to 640×512 in two colors, or 256 colors at a lower horizontal resolution. Its custom 'Dave' sound chip provided three channels plus a noise generator. The Enterprise ran IS-BASIC, an unusual structured BASIC interpreter. Despite impressive specifications, the machine arrived too late to compete effectively - it was announced in 1983 but delays meant it didn't ship until 1985, by which time the market was dominated by established machines. The Enterprise found a loyal following in Hungary, where it remained popular well into the 1990s.

historicalNotes.title: Konami's Golden Age
historicalNotes.text: The MSX2 was Konami's primary development platform during their golden age. Metal Gear, Vampire Killer, and Snatcher all debuted on MSX2. Hideo Kojima considers the MSX2 versions of his games the definitive ones.

historicalNotes.title: The 1985 Standard
historicalNotes.text: Introduced in 1985, MSX2 substantially upgraded the original MSX with better graphics hardware, more video RAM, and a software culture that increasingly assumed floppy-disk drives rather than cassette tapes.

historicalNotes.title: One Standard, Many Brands
historicalNotes.text: Because MSX was a common standard rather than a single manufacturer's platform, MSX2 software could run across machines from Panasonic, Sony, Philips, and many others.

overview: The MSX2 (1985) was the second generation of the MSX standard, featuring significantly upgraded graphics through the Yamaha V9938 video display processor. It offered 256×212 resolution with 256 simultaneous colors from a palette of 512, hardware scrolling, and a bitmap graphics mode - major improvements over the original MSX. With 64-128 KB RAM and often a built-in 3.5-inch floppy drive, MSX2 machines became the platform of choice for Japanese game developers. Konami produced many of their finest 8-bit titles for the MSX2, including Metal Gear and Vampire Killer (a unique take on the Castlevania series).

historicalNotes.title: Spain Got It First
historicalNotes.text: The first Spectrum 128 launched in Spain in 1985 through distributor Investrónica, before the British release. That unusual rollout showed just how important the Spanish market had become to Sinclair by the mid-1980s.

historicalNotes.title: The Sound of 128K Gaming
historicalNotes.text: The AY-3-8912 sound chip transformed the Spectrum from simple beeps to proper three-channel music. Later 128K versions of games used the extra RAM for larger levels, richer loading systems, and lavish menu music that 48K owners could only envy.

historicalNotes.title: A Compatibility Tightrope
historicalNotes.text: Its startup menu let users choose between new 128K software and a 48K compatibility mode, acknowledging that the old software library was far too valuable to abandon. That backward compatibility helped the Spectrum line survive into the Amstrad years.

overview: The ZX Spectrum 128 (1985/1986) was developed in collaboration with the Spanish distributor Investrónica and launched in Spain before the UK. It doubled the RAM to 128 KB (bank-switched), added an AY-3-8912 sound chip for three-channel music, included an RS-232 serial port and MIDI interface, and featured a redesigned ROM with a startup menu. It represented the most significant technical upgrade in the Spectrum line.

historicalNotes.title: Graphics and Sound
historicalNotes.text: The 'GS' stood for Graphics and Sound - Steve Wozniak's final contribution to the Apple II line. The Ensoniq 5503 DOC chip provided 32 oscillators of wavetable synthesis, making it one of the most musically capable home computers. However, Apple deliberately limited the CPU speed to avoid cannibalizing Macintosh sales.

historicalNotes.title: The Last Apple II
historicalNotes.text: Despite being technologically superior to the early Macintosh in many ways, Apple corporate ensured the IIGS never reached its full potential. Its 2.8 MHz clock speed was reportedly set artificially low, and Apple focused development resources on the Mac platform, eventually discontinuing the IIGS in 1992.

"GS" stood for Graphics and Sound. $999, approximately 1 million sold.

historicalNotes.title: Continuing the Educational Legacy
historicalNotes.text: The BBC Master continued the BBC Micro's dominance in UK schools throughout the late 1980s. Many schools upgraded from the Model B to the Master, taking advantage of the extra memory and improved filing system while retaining their existing software libraries.

historicalNotes.title: Acorn's 1986 Refresh
historicalNotes.text: Launched in 1986, the Master 128 was Acorn's final major update to the BBC Micro family. It kept the BBC platform commercially relevant while Acorn prepared the newer ARM-based Archimedes line.

historicalNotes.title: Shadow RAM Matters
historicalNotes.text: One of the Master series' most practical improvements was shadow RAM, which moved screen memory out of the main program area. That left more working space free for BBC BASIC, educational software, and disc-based applications.

overview: The BBC Master, launched in 1986 by Acorn Computers, was the successor to the hugely successful BBC Micro. Powered by a 65C02 processor running at 2 MHz with 128 KB of RAM, it offered significant improvements over its predecessor while maintaining backward compatibility with most BBC Micro software. The Master featured an improved filing system, built-in word processor and spreadsheet in ROM, and better expansion options. It continued the BBC Micro's dominance in UK education and sold approximately 200,000 units, remaining in use in schools well into the 1990s.

historicalNotes.title: Made for Minitel
historicalNotes.text: The Telestrat was designed around France's Minitel network, one of the world's most successful pre-web online services. Its serial connection to a Minitel terminal and telematics software supported online use without a built-in modem.

historicalNotes.title: An Afterlife for Oric
historicalNotes.text: The Telestrat arrived after Oric's earlier financial troubles and was produced in relatively small numbers. That makes it both a technological curiosity and the last serious attempt to keep the Oric platform commercially alive.

overview: The Oric Telestrat, released in 1986 by ASN Computers (successor to Oric Products International), was a uniquely French take on the home computer. Built around the 6502 processor at 1 MHz with 64 KB of RAM, it provided a serial connection to a Minitel terminal for use with France's videotex network - years before internet connectivity became standard in home computers. It used the same graphics capabilities as earlier Oric machines and featured the AY-3-8912 sound chip. With Hyper BASIC and telematic software in ROM, plus a supplied external 3-inch Microdisc drive, the Telestrat was designed for the connected French home. Only around 3,000 units were produced, making it one of the rarest home computers of the era.

historicalNotes.title: OS-9: A Multitasking Marvel
historicalNotes.text: The CoCo 3 could run OS-9 Level II, a Unix-like multitasking operating system that was remarkably sophisticated for an 8-bit computer. With its expanded memory and improved graphics, the CoCo 3 running OS-9 offered capabilities that rivaled far more expensive machines.

historicalNotes.title: The 1986 High Point
historicalNotes.text: Released in 1986, the CoCo 3 is usually seen as the peak of the Color Computer family, pairing new graphics hardware with much more memory than earlier models.

historicalNotes.title: Compatibility Was the Strategy
historicalNotes.text: Tandy preserved substantial compatibility with earlier CoCo software, letting owners bring their existing BASIC programs, cartridges, and many games forward to the new machine.

overview: The Tandy Color Computer 3, released in 1986, was a major upgrade to the CoCo line. Powered by the Motorola 68B09E at 1.79 MHz (double the original CoCo's speed) with 128 KB of RAM expandable to 512 KB, it offered significantly improved graphics including 320×225 in 16 colors and up to 640×225 resolution. historicalNotes.title: Tape's Last Big Stand

historicalNotes.title: The First ARM Computer
historicalNotes.text: The Archimedes was the first production computer to use the ARM (Acorn RISC Machine) processor. The ARM architecture, originally designed for Acorn's desktop computers, went on to become the most widely used processor architecture in the world, powering billions of smartphones, tablets, and embedded devices.

historicalNotes.title: Desktop Performance Leader
historicalNotes.text: When launched in 1987, the Archimedes was arguably the fastest desktop computer available, outperforming machines costing many times more. David Braben's Zarch demo, bundled with early machines as Lander, showcased 3D graphics capabilities that stunned the computing press.

photos.caption: The Acorn Archimedes - the groundbreaking ARM-powered machine that outpaced its rivals

overview: The Acorn Archimedes, launched in 1987, brought ARM-based desktop computing to a wider audience. Using the ARM2 processor running at 8 MHz - designed in-house by Sophie Wilson and Steve Furber - it offered strong performance for its price. The first models shipped with Arthur; RISC OS 2 followed in 1989 with a cooperative-multitasking desktop. The Archimedes demonstrated the extraordinary potential of the ARM architecture, which today powers virtually every smartphone on Earth. Approximately 100,000 units were sold, primarily into UK education, where it succeeded the BBC Micro.

historicalNotes.text: The Amiga 500 brought the revolutionary Amiga technology to the masses. While the Amiga 1000 had been expensive and positioned as a professional machine, the A500's keyboard-integrated design and $699 price point made it the best-selling Amiga model. In Europe, it became the dominant home computer, outselling the Atari ST and rivaling PC compatibles for gaming.
historicalNotes.title: The People's Amiga

historicalNotes.text: The original Amiga 1000 (1985) had a distinctive IBM PC compatibility expansion called the 'Sidecar' - a bulky unit that sat to the right of the machine, adding an 8086 coprocessor, 256 KB of RAM, and a 5.25-inch floppy drive to run MS-DOS software. It was expensive and sold in limited numbers, but it demonstrated the Amiga team's confidence that their machine could absorb an entire PC as a peripheral.
historicalNotes.title: The Amiga 1000's Sidecar

historicalNotes.text: The A500's left-side trapdoor and rear expansion port spawned a thriving industry. The trapdoor slot (originally designed for a 512 KB RAM expansion) was exploited by products like the Action Replay cartridge and a variety of memory/clock combinations. More ambitious were the hard drive units that clipped beneath the machine - brands like GVP (Great Valley Products) and Supra offered SCSI or IDE drives in self-powered cases that extended the A500's footprint. Genlocks let the Amiga composite its graphics over live video, making the A500 a genuine desktop video production tool. Sound samplers (Technosound Turbo, Amas) and video digitisers (Digi-View, Rombo Vidi Amiga) rounded out an ecosystem that made the A500 genuinely versatile far beyond gaming.
historicalNotes.title: The Expansion Bay

overview: The Commodore Amiga 500, released in 1987, was the 'people's Amiga' - a more affordable version of the groundbreaking Amiga 1000 in a compact all-in-one keyboard design. Powered by the same Motorola MC68000 at 7.16 MHz with 512 KB of RAM, it featured the custom Agnus, Denise, and Paula chipset providing hardware-accelerated graphics with 4096 colors, four-channel stereo PCM sound, and a built-in 3.5-inch floppy drive. At $699, the A500 made the Amiga's multimedia capabilities accessible to a mass market. It became the best-selling Amiga model and dominated the European home computer market, particularly in the UK and Germany, where it was the machine of choice for gaming and creative applications.

historicalNotes.title: Color Changes Everything
historicalNotes.text: The Macintosh II's introduction of color transformed the Mac from a niche business machine into the dominant platform for desktop publishing and graphic design. The combination of color graphics, NuBus expansion, and PostScript laser printing created the desktop publishing revolution that kept Apple profitable through difficult years.

historicalNotes.title: Breaking the Compact Mold
historicalNotes.text: The Macintosh II abandoned the original all-in-one Mac form factor for a modular desktop case with a separate monitor and expansion cards, a major philosophical shift for Apple in 1987.

historicalNotes.title: The High-End Creative Mac
historicalNotes.text: Its blend of color, large memory capacity, and NuBus expansion made it the Mac of choice for graphics, prepress, scientific, and other high-end professional users.

overview: The Apple Macintosh II, also released in March 1987, was a revolutionary departure for Apple. It was the first Macintosh with color graphics, a modular design with NuBus expansion slots, and a separate monitor. Powered by the Motorola MC68020 at 16 MHz with 1 MB of RAM expandable to a then-staggering 68 MB, it could drive displays up to 1024×768 with 16.7 million colors through third-party NuBus video cards. At $5,498 (without monitor), it was expensive but established the Mac as a serious platform for desktop publishing, graphic design, and scientific computing. The Mac II architecture influenced Apple's product line for years to come.

This single SE Bus slot could accept accelerator cards, Ethernet adapters, or additional video cards, making the SE far more versatile than its predecessors.

historicalNotes.title: The 1987 Mac Refresh
historicalNotes.text: Apple introduced the Macintosh SE in March 1987 alongside the Macintosh II, giving the Mac line a major hardware refresh after three years of compact all-in-one models.

historicalNotes.title: A Desktop Publishing Workhorse
historicalNotes.text: With SCSI hard-disk options and a compact, reliable design, the SE became a popular office and desktop-publishing Macintosh in the late 1980s.

overview: The Apple Macintosh SE, released in March 1987, was a significant evolution of the compact Macintosh design. The 'SE' stood for System Expansion, referring to its internal expansion slot - a first for the compact Mac line. Powered by a Motorola MC68000 at 8 MHz with 1 MB of RAM (expandable to 4 MB), it featured the same 512×342 monochrome display as its predecessors but added an optional internal 20 MB hard disk. The SE's expansion slot and SCSI port made it far more versatile than earlier compact Macs, and it became a workhorse in offices and schools throughout the late 1980s.
