historicalNotes.title: A Laptop Before Laptops
historicalNotes.text: The Z88 gave writers and journalists something rare in 1987: a genuinely usable battery-powered computer with instant-on operation and exceptional endurance. In spirit it was far closer to a modern ultraportable than to the mains-powered 'luggables' that usually counted as portable computing at the time.

historicalNotes.title: OZ Was Years Ahead
historicalNotes.text: Its OZ operating system let users jump between applications without closing them, with documents and sessions preserved in memory. That kind of seamless task switching felt astonishingly modern on an 8-bit machine.

photos.caption: The Cambridge Z88 portable computer
Sir Clive Sinclair with the Cambridge Z88
The Z88 has only four chips: a Z80, a ROM for the OS, some RAM, and a custom ASIC
How the Z88 is laid out inside
Close-up of the Cambridge Z88 - designed by Rick Dickinson

overview:
The Cambridge Z88 (1987) was the last computer from Clive Sinclair's post-Amstrad company, Cambridge Computer. Its elegant industrial design was the work of Rick Dickinson - the same designer responsible for the iconic look of the ZX81, ZX Spectrum, and Sinclair QL. A remarkable portable machine weighing under 1 kg with an integrated LCD display, full-size membrane keyboard, and powered by 4 AA batteries lasting up to 20 hours. It ran a CMOS Z80 at 3.2768 MHz with 32 KB RAM expandable via cartridge slots.

The Z88 ran OZ, a sophisticated multitasking operating system that was far ahead of its time. OZ allowed users to suspend and resume multiple applications simultaneously - switching instantly between the word processor, spreadsheet, diary, calculator, and BBC BASIC with a single keypress. Each application preserved its state perfectly, behaving much like modern mobile operating systems decades before smartphones.

Three cartridge slots on the front accepted EPROM and Flash memory cards for additional storage and software. RAM cards (up to 1 MB each) provided working memory, while EPROM cards held applications or served as permanent file storage. This card-based architecture made the Z88 highly expandable despite its slim profile. It was used by journalists, authors, and travelers who valued its exceptional battery life and instant-on convenience.

historicalNotes.text: The KC 87 showed how East German home computing kept evolving even under tight economic and technological limits. It refined the KC line rather than reinventing it, squeezing more usefulness out of the same basic Eastern Bloc component world.

historicalNotes.title: School and Club Machine
historicalNotes.text: Like other Robotron micros, the KC 87 mattered as much in schools and youth clubs as in private homes. That institutional role helped sustain programming communities in the DDR even when consumer availability remained limited.

overview: The Robotron KC 87, released in 1987, was an improved member of VEB Robotron's KC (KleinComputer) series of home computers produced in East Germany. Using the U880 processor (a Z80 clone) at 2.5 MHz with 16 to 48 KB of RAM, it developed Robotron's earlier KC 85/1 (Z9001) design, not the incompatible Mühlhausen KC 85/2–85/4 family. The KC 87 featured a 40×24 text display with pseudo-graphics capabilities and used cassette tape for storage. Many machines went to schools, youth clubs, and workplaces, with limited availability for private buyers. The KC 87 represented the continued evolution of East German home computing technology despite the constraints of COCOM restrictions on Western technology imports.

historicalNotes.title: The Arcade at Home
historicalNotes.text: The X68000 was so close to arcade hardware that Capcom used it as a development platform for their CPS-1 arcade board. Games like Street Fighter II and Final Fight were developed on X68000 hardware, resulting in home ports that were virtually indistinguishable from their arcade counterparts.

historicalNotes.title: Capcom's Development Platform
historicalNotes.text: Sharp's partnership with Capcom was pivotal. Many CPS-1 arcade titles were developed on X68000 hardware before being ported to arcade boards, making the X68000 the only home platform capable of truly arcade-perfect ports during the late 1980s and early 1990s.

overview: The Sharp X68000, released in 1987, was a powerful home computer that became the dominant gaming PC in Japan. Built around the Motorola MC68000 CPU running at 10 MHz with 1-4 MB of RAM, it featured custom graphics hardware capable of 768×512 resolution with 65,536 colors and hardware sprite support rivaling arcade machines. Its YM2151 FM synthesis chip paired with PCM sound produced arcade-quality audio. Priced at ¥369,000, the X68000 became famous for arcade-perfect ports, and many arcade games - including Capcom's CPS-1 titles - were actually developed on X68000 hardware before being ported to arcade boards.

historicalNotes.title: The Disk Drive Dream
historicalNotes.text: For years Spectrum owners had lived with cassettes or expensive third-party disk systems; the +3 finally made floppy drives standard. Built-in +3DOS and CP/M turned it into the closest thing the Spectrum line ever had to a proper disk-based home computer.

historicalNotes.title: The Trouble with 3-Inch Disks
historicalNotes.text: Amstrad chose the same 3-inch drives used in the CPC range, which were sturdy but more expensive and less common than 3.5-inch media. The result was a technically neat machine tied to an awkward format just as the wider industry was standardising elsewhere.

historicalNotes.title: The Last Official Spectrum
historicalNotes.text: The +3 was the end of the official Spectrum line, and in some ways its most capable form. But by 1987 the centre of gravity in British gaming had shifted toward the Amiga and Atari ST, leaving the +3 as a brilliant late flourish rather than a fresh beginning.

overview: The ZX Spectrum +3 (1987) was the final official Spectrum model. It included an updated +3DOS operating system, could run CP/M, and had 64 KB of ROM. It was the most capable Spectrum but arrived as the market shifted to 16-bit machines.

historicalNotes.title: Birthplace of the World Wide Web
historicalNotes.text: In 1989-1990, Tim Berners-Lee, working at CERN, used a NeXT Computer to develop the first web browser (WorldWideWeb) and web server (httpd). The NeXT's advanced development tools - particularly Interface Builder and Objective-C - made it possible for Berners-Lee to create these foundational technologies relatively quickly.

historicalNotes.title: From NeXTSTEP to macOS
historicalNotes.text: When Apple acquired NeXT in 1997 for $429 million, it was NeXTSTEP that proved most valuable. The operating system was modernized into Mac OS X (now macOS), and its frameworks - including Objective-C and later Swift - became the foundation of iOS, watchOS, and all of Apple's modern platforms.

photos.caption: NeXT advertisement introducing its computer and workstation environment

overview: The NeXT Computer, released in 1988, was Steve Jobs' vision of the perfect workstation after his departure from Apple. Built around a Motorola MC68030 at 25 MHz with 8 MB of RAM, it featured a stunning 1120×832 monochrome MegaPixel display, a Motorola DSP56001 for CD-quality sound, and a pioneering 256 MB magneto-optical drive. The NeXT ran NeXTSTEP, an object-oriented operating system built on the Mach kernel that was years ahead of its time. At $6,500 it was too expensive for its target academic market, but its software legacy was enormous: Tim Berners-Lee created the World Wide Web on a NeXT, and NeXTSTEP eventually evolved into macOS, iOS, and the foundation of Apple's modern operating systems.

historicalNotes.title: Amstrad in German Clothes
historicalNotes.text: Amstrad sold computers under the Schneider name in German-speaking markets, so the Euro PC was effectively an Amstrad strategy tailored for West Germany. It gave home-computer buyers a familiar, approachable path into IBM compatibility.

historicalNotes.title: A Budget PC for the Mail-Order Era
historicalNotes.text: The Euro PC sold strongly through German mail-order and consumer-electronics channels because it looked simpler and cheaper than corporate PCs. Its compact all-in-keyboard design and aggressive pricing helped bring MS-DOS computing into small offices and bedrooms.

overview: The Schneider Euro PC (1988) was an IBM PC-compatible computer sold under the Schneider brand, which was Amstrad's trade name in the German-speaking market. Powered by an Intel 8088 processor running at 9.54 MHz, it came with 512 KB of RAM, CGA and Hercules-compatible graphics, a PC speaker for sound, and a built-in 3.5-inch floppy drive. Priced at 999 DM (approximately $600), it was one of the most affordable IBM-compatible computers available in Germany and played an important role in bringing PC compatibility to German homes and small offices at a time when genuine IBM PCs remained prohibitively expensive.

historicalNotes.title: The Enhanced ST Dilemma
historicalNotes.text: The STE's enhanced hardware capabilities - including DMA sound, hardware scrolling, and a blitter chip - were impressive, but the installed base of original STs was so large that few developers created STE-specific software. Most games and applications continued to target the original ST specification for maximum compatibility.

historicalNotes.title: Atari's 1989 Refresh
historicalNotes.text: The STe arrived in 1989 as Atari's answer to long-standing complaints about the original ST's limited sampled sound and scrolling hardware.

historicalNotes.title: Beloved by Demos and Music
historicalNotes.text: Although commercial software support was patchy, the STe's DMA audio and improved graphics made it especially attractive for sample-based music tools and later demo-scene productions.

overview: The Atari STE, released in 1989, was an enhanced version of the ST featuring improved hardware for gaming and multimedia. It added a BLiTTER chip for faster graphics operations, hardware scrolling, an extended color palette with 4096 colors, and DMA stereo 8-bit PCM sound alongside the existing YM2149. With 512 KB to 4 MB of RAM and enhanced joystick ports supporting analog input, the STE was better suited to gaming than the original ST. However, relatively few software titles took advantage of the enhanced features, as developers preferred to maintain compatibility with the larger installed base of original ST users.

historicalNotes.title: The First CD-ROM Computer
historicalNotes.text: The FM Towns was the world's first personal computer to ship with a built-in CD-ROM drive in 1989, years before CD-ROMs became standard in PCs. This gave FM Towns software access to 540 MB of storage - enormous compared to the 1.2 MB floppy disks of the era.

historicalNotes.title: Fujitsu's Multimedia Vision
historicalNotes.text: Fujitsu designed the FM Towns as a multimedia powerhouse, combining high-color graphics, FM synthesis, PCM audio, and CD-DA playback. This vision of multimedia computing predated similar efforts by Apple and Microsoft by several years.

overview: The Fujitsu FM Towns, released in 1989, holds the distinction of being the world's first personal computer with a built-in CD-ROM drive. Powered by an Intel 80386DX CPU at 16 MHz with 2 MB of RAM, it offered 640×480 graphics and lower-resolution modes with 32,768 simultaneous colors, plus a powerful sound system combining Yamaha YM2612 FM synthesis, PCM channels, and CD-DA audio. Priced at ¥338,000, the FM Towns was Fujitsu's vision of multimedia computing, and its CD-ROM capabilities allowed for games and software with full voice acting, CD-quality music, and rich graphical content years before CD-ROM became standard on PCs.

historicalNotes.title: The Spectrum Heir Apparent
historicalNotes.text: Miles Gordon Technology pitched the SAM Coupé as the natural upgrade for Spectrum owners: familiar Z80 roots, broad compatibility, but vastly more RAM, colour, and sound. On paper it was exactly the kind of bridge the British 8-bit market had been waiting for.

historicalNotes.title: Too Late for 8-Bit Glory
historicalNotes.text: When the SAM finally shipped in late 1989, cheap Amigas and Atari STs had already pushed the market toward 16-bit machines. Reviewers respected the hardware, but its timing was disastrous and sales never matched the ambition.

historicalNotes.title: Built by Peripheral Experts
historicalNotes.text: MGT had already earned a strong reputation with Spectrum disk systems such as the DISCiPLE and +D. That experience showed in the SAM's serious approach to storage and expandability, making it feel like an 8-bit computer designed by people who knew exactly what enthusiasts had been bolting onto Spectrums for years.

overview: The SAM Coupé, released in late 1989 by Miles Gordon Technology of Swansea, Wales, was designed as a logical upgrade from the ZX Spectrum. It could run most Spectrum software in a compatibility mode while offering significantly enhanced capabilities: a 6 MHz Z80B, 256 KB RAM, 128 colors, and the SAA1099 six-channel sound chip. Its screen modes included a Spectrum-compatible mode and a high-color mode with 4 pixels per byte. Despite being technically impressive, it arrived too late to compete with 16-bit machines like the Amiga and Atari ST, and MGT went bankrupt in 1992.

historicalNotes.title: A Macintosh Below $1,000
historicalNotes.text: Apple introduced the Classic on October 15, 1990, alongside the Macintosh LC and IIsi. The $999 US base price lowered the entry cost of owning a Mac, but bought a floppy-only system with 1 MB RAM. The $1,499 configuration included 2 MB RAM and a 40 MB hard disk.

historicalNotes.title: Familiar Technology, Different Priorities
historicalNotes.text: The Classic retained the 68000 processor and 512×342 monochrome screen associated with earlier compact Macs. A high-density SuperDrive, ADB input devices, and SCSI made it more practical than the original 128K, but its 8 MHz CPU and 4 MB memory ceiling limited demanding work. Unlike the SE, it offered no internal expansion slot.

historicalNotes.title: Classic Is Not Classic II
historicalNotes.text: The original Classic dates to 1990, even when a surviving example or artwork is labeled 1991. Apple introduced the separate Classic II on October 21, 1991 with a 16 MHz 68030, 2 MB of base RAM, and a 10 MB maximum. The original Classic remained in Apple's range until September 1992.

historicalNotes.title: A Desktop Hidden in ROM
historicalNotes.text: Alongside its normal disk-based operating system, the Classic's 512 KB ROM contains a small System 6.0.3 environment, accessible by holding Command-Option-X-O at startup. This unusual feature is distinct from the System 6.0.7 software originally supplied on disk.

overview:
Introduced on October 15, 1990, the Apple Macintosh Classic brought the compact Mac experience to a lower price: the entry-level configuration cost $999 in the United States. Its all-in-one case contained a 9-inch monochrome display, an 8 MHz Motorola 68000 processor, and a 1.44 MB SuperDrive. The base model had 1 MB of RAM and no hard disk; a $1,499 configuration paired 2 MB with a 40 MB internal SCSI drive.

The Classic emphasized affordability and compatibility rather than speed. Its 512×342 desktop suited word processing, schoolwork, and established black-and-white Mac software. Apple Desktop Bus connected the keyboard and mouse, while SCSI and serial ports provided storage, printing, and LocalTalk networking. It shipped with System 6.0.7 and could run later System 7 releases with sufficient memory, up to System 7.5.5.

Despite the familiar silhouette, this was a separate model from the 1984 Macintosh 128K and the 1987 Macintosh SE. It also lacked the SE's internal expansion slot. The Macintosh Classic II, introduced in October 1991, was a different machine with a 16 MHz 68030 and 2 MB of base RAM; those specifications do not apply to the original Classic.

historicalNotes.title: The End of MSX
historicalNotes.text: The MSX turbo R was the final evolution of the MSX standard. Only Panasonic produced turbo R machines - the FS-A1ST (1990) and FS-A1GT (1991). By this time, 16-bit computers and game consoles had overtaken the MSX market. Despite this, MSX maintains a devoted following, and MSX hardware and software development continues in the retro computing community.

historicalNotes.title: The R800 Leap
historicalNotes.text: The turbo R replaced the classic Z80 with ASCII Corporation's much faster R800 CPU while preserving compatibility with earlier MSX software, making it the fastest standard MSX ever sold.

historicalNotes.title: A Japan-Only Farewell
historicalNotes.text: The turbo R was sold only in Japan, and by 1990 the market had shifted so far toward consoles and 16-bit computers that it could only serve as a final flourish for the standard.

overview: The MSX turbo R, released by Panasonic in 1990, was the final and most powerful generation of the MSX standard. It featured the custom R800 processor running at 7.16 MHz alongside a Z80A for backward compatibility, with 256 to 512 KB of RAM. The turbo R used the Yamaha V9958 video chip offering 256×212 resolution with 19,268 simultaneous colors and MSX-MUSIC FM synthesis for rich audio. With a built-in 3.5-inch floppy drive and MSX-DOS2 operating system, it was the most capable MSX ever produced. However, by 1990 the MSX standard was losing ground to more powerful platforms, and only Panasonic produced turbo R machines (the FS-A1ST and FS-A1GT models). The turbo R marked the end of the MSX line.

historicalNotes.title: Commodore's Swan Song
historicalNotes.text: The Amiga 1200 represented the pinnacle of Commodore's engineering, with the AGA chipset pushing the Amiga's custom hardware philosophy to new heights. But by 1992, Commodore was financially struggling and couldn't invest in adequate marketing. The company went bankrupt in 1994, just two years after the A1200's release, ending one of computing's most innovative lineages.

historicalNotes.title: Accelerator Cards
historicalNotes.text: The A1200's trapdoor expansion slot became the foundation of a flourishing accelerator industry. Companies like Blizzard (Phase 5), Apollo, and Microbotics released cards ranging from simple 68020/030 FPUs with fast RAM up to full 68060 accelerators running at 50 MHz - turning the entry-level A1200 into a machine that outperformed workstations costing many times more. Many cards included additional fast RAM (up to 128 MB), SCSI controllers, and even network interfaces. The accelerator scene has continued into the 21st century, with modern FPGA-based 'vampire' accelerators offering performance beyond any 68k chip ever made.

overview: The Commodore Amiga 1200, released in 1992, was the last great Amiga. Powered by a Motorola MC68EC020 at 14 MHz with 2 MB of Chip RAM, it featured the AGA (Advanced Graphics Architecture) chipset offering 256 colors from a palette of 16.8 million, with resolutions up to 1280×512. AGA was a major step forward from the original OCS/ECS chipset: it expanded the color palette from 4,096 to 16.8 million colors, increased the maximum displayable colors per screen from 64 (in HAM6) to 256 in standard modes and 262,144 in HAM8 mode, doubled sprite width to 64 pixels, added support for higher bandwidth data fetching for smoother scrolling, and introduced scan-doubled productivity modes for flicker-free output on VGA monitors. These improvements made the A1200 genuinely competitive with contemporary PCs for gaming and video work. The A1200 maintained the keyboard-integrated design of the A500 while adding a PCMCIA slot, IDE hard disk interface, and a trapdoor expansion slot for accelerator cards. At $599, it was competitive on price, but by 1992 Commodore was in financial trouble and couldn't market it effectively. Despite this, the A1200 developed a devoted following and remains popular in the retro computing community.

historicalNotes.title: The Compact Amiga
historicalNotes.text: The A600 was designed as an entry-level replacement for the A500, but Commodore misjudged the market. Its smaller size cost it the numeric keypad, and its price was only marginally lower than the far superior A1200, which launched the same year. The PCMCIA slot was innovative but rarely exploited. The A600 is fondly remembered today as the most pocketable 'real' Amiga - a curiosity that time has been kinder to than the market was.

historicalNotes.title: A 1992 Replacement Attempt
historicalNotes.text: Commodore launched the A600 in 1992 as a smaller successor to the Amiga 500, but many buyers saw it as a sideways move rather than a meaningful performance upgrade.

historicalNotes.title: A Better Storage Platform
historicalNotes.text: Its built-in IDE and PCMCIA support later made the A600 especially attractive to hobbyists fitting solid-state storage, memory cards, and even network adapters - conveniences earlier low-end Amigas lacked.

overview: The Commodore Amiga 600, released in 1992, was Commodore's attempt to offer a compact, budget-priced Amiga using the Enhanced Chip Set (ECS). Smaller than the A500, it retained the OCS/ECS chipset of its predecessor but added a built-in IDE interface for a 2.5-inch hard disk and - uniquely for an Amiga of its era - a PCMCIA Type II slot. It shipped with 1 MB of Chip RAM and Kickstart 2.05, offering a more modern AmigaOS experience. Unfortunately, Commodore omitted the numeric keypad, and the A600 launched at a price that made the more powerful A1200 a far better value. It sold modestly but is fondly remembered as the most compact full-featured Amiga ever made.

historicalNotes.title: One of the Last Z80 Computers
historicalNotes.text: By 1992, the Z80 processor family was decades old, but Amstrad found a perfect niche for it in the NC100 - a simple, affordable portable writing machine. Its incredible battery life and instant-on capability made it popular with journalists and writers who needed a distraction-free tool.

historicalNotes.title: An Electronic Notebook, Not a Laptop
historicalNotes.text: Amstrad pitched the NC100 as a low-cost electronic notebook rather than a DOS-compatible laptop. Its instant-on behavior and battery-backed RAM made it feel closer to a digital typewriter than to a conventional portable PC.

historicalNotes.title: A Writer's Favorite
historicalNotes.text: The quiet operation, full-size keyboard, and built-in BBC BASIC gave the NC100 a loyal following among journalists, students, and hobbyist programmers. Long after release, many users still regarded it as one of the best pure writing machines Amstrad ever made.

overview: The Amstrad NC100, released in 1992, was a portable Z80-based notepad computer designed for writing on the go. Powered by a Z80 processor at 4.606 MHz with 64 KB of RAM, it featured a built-in word processor, BBC BASIC interpreter, address book, diary, and calculator. Notably, its BBC BASIC included a built-in Z80 assembler - just like the BBC Micro's BASIC had a 6502 assembler - allowing programmers to write machine code directly from the BASIC environment. Its non-backlit LCD displayed 80×8 characters, and it could run for up to 20 hours on four AA batteries. The NC100 was one of the last significant Z80-based computers to reach the market, offering a simple, affordable alternative to expensive laptops for basic writing tasks.

historicalNotes.title: Atari's Final Computer
historicalNotes.text: The Falcon030 was the last computer Atari ever produced. Despite its impressive specifications - including a Motorola DSP56001 for real-time audio processing - Atari under the Tramiel family was already shifting focus to the Jaguar game console. The Falcon was produced in limited quantities, primarily in the Braun AG factory in Germany, before Atari exited the computer market entirely in 1993.

historicalNotes.title: A Brief 1992 Debut
historicalNotes.text: Introduced in 1992, the Falcon030 was Atari's most advanced desktop computer, but it remained on the market for only a short time before the company abandoned the computer business.

historicalNotes.title: A Cult Afterlife
historicalNotes.text: Its DSP, multichannel audio features, and strong MIDI heritage gave the Falcon a long afterlife in music production and the European demo scene.

overview: The Atari Falcon030, released in 1992, was the last computer produced by Atari. Powered by a Motorola MC68030 at 16 MHz paired with a Motorola DSP56001 digital signal processor, it offered impressive multimedia capabilities including True Color (65,536 colors) graphics, 16-bit stereo sound, and advanced DSP-based audio processing. With 1 to 14 MB of RAM and an IDE hard disk interface, the Falcon was technically competitive with contemporary PCs. The built-in DSP made it particularly attractive for music production, continuing the ST's legacy in professional audio. However, Atari's focus shifted to the Jaguar game console, and the Falcon was produced in limited quantities before Atari exited the computer market entirely.

historicalNotes.title: A PC With a Mega Drive Inside
historicalNotes.text: Amstrad built the Mega PC with Sega to combine a DOS computer and a Mega Drive in one case, years before 'convergence' became a standard industry buzzword. It was an unusually literal attempt to sell one machine to both parents and children.

historicalNotes.title: Too Early, Too Expensive
historicalNotes.text: The idea was memorable, but the timing was bad: the PC side was underpowered for the price, and a separate console was far cheaper. That made the Mega PC famous as a curiosity rather than successful as a product.

overview: The Amstrad Mega PC, released in 1993, was one of the most unusual computers ever produced - a hybrid machine combining a fully functional IBM PC compatible (Intel 386SX at 25 MHz with 1 MB RAM) and a Sega Mega Drive game console in a desktop case. Users could switch between PC mode and Mega Drive mode using the supplied dual-frequency monitor. Priced at £999 in the UK, it was Alan Sugar's attempt to create an all-in-one family entertainment and computing solution. The concept was ahead of its time but the execution was poor - the PC specs were already outdated, and the premium price for an integrated Mega Drive wasn't compelling when standalone consoles cost far less. Very few units were sold, making it a rare collector's item today.

historicalNotes.text: Those upgrades also made the NC200 heavier, more expensive, and less frugal on batteries. As a result, it never matched the NC100's reputation as the sweet spot of Amstrad's notepad line.

historicalNotes.title: Bondi Blue Shockwave
historicalNotes.text: Jony Ive's translucent Bondi Blue shell made the iMac G3 instantly recognizable and turned the beige PC box into a relic overnight. Apple later expanded the line into 13 colorful 'flavors,' but the original Bondi Blue machine remains the icon that redefined late-1990s industrial design.

historicalNotes.title: USB-Only Gamble
historicalNotes.text: The iMac G3 dropped the floppy drive, SCSI, serial ports, and ADB in one stroke, betting entirely on USB at a time when many peripherals still depended on legacy connectors. The move was widely criticized at launch, yet it accelerated industry-wide adoption of USB faster than any previous consumer computer.

historicalNotes.title: Apple's Comeback Machine
historicalNotes.text: The iMac's strong sales gave Apple desperately needed momentum during Steve Jobs' return, proving the company could still create products people desired. More than a successful computer, it restored Apple's confidence, revived its brand, and set the stage for the iBook, iPod, and the design-first era that followed.

overview: The Apple iMac G3, announced by Steve Jobs on May 6, 1998 and shipped on August 15, 1998, was the computer that signaled Apple's comeback. Designed by Jony Ive as a translucent Bondi Blue all-in-one, it combined a 233 MHz PowerPC G3 processor, built-in 15-inch CRT display, 4 GB hard drive, and 24x CD-ROM in a friendly consumer appliance that put the internet front and center. Its bold decision to drop the floppy drive, ADB, serial, and SCSI ports in favor of USB-only connectivity was controversial, but it helped push USB into the mainstream and reset expectations for industrial design across the entire technology industry.
